title: Selection Sort
description: Given an array of integers, sort it in ascending order using the selection sort algorithm. On each pass, select the minimum element from the unsorted suffix and swap it into its final position. The array is modified in place.

examples.explanation: Pass 1 swaps 11 with 64, pass 2 swaps 12 with 25, and so on until the array is sorted.

title: Bubble Sort
description: Given an array of integers, sort it in ascending order using bubble sort. Repeatedly step through the array, swap adjacent elements that are out of order, and repeat until a full pass makes no swaps. The largest remaining element bubbles to the end of the array on every pass.

examples.explanation: 8 bubbles to the end on the first pass, then 5, 4 and so on until no swaps remain.

title: Insertion Sorting
description: Given an array of integers, sort it in ascending order using insertion sort. Grow a sorted prefix one element at a time by shifting each new element left into its correct position, the way you would sort playing cards in your hand.

examples.explanation: 11 shifts before 12, then 5 is inserted at the front, and finally 6 slots between 5 and 11.

title: Merge Sorting
description: Given an array of integers, sort it in ascending order using merge sort. Recursively split the array into halves until single elements remain, then merge the sorted halves back together in linear time. The algorithm must run in O(n log n) time.

examples.explanation: Split into [38, 27] and [43, 10], recursively sort them to [27, 38] and [10, 43], then merge.

title: Recursive Bubble Sort
description: Sort an array in ascending order with a recursive formulation of bubble sort. One recursion level performs a single bubbling pass that pushes the largest element of the current range to its end, then recurses on the remaining prefix. The base case is a range of length 0 or 1.

title: Recursive Insertion Sort
description: Sort an array in ascending order with a recursive formulation of insertion sort. Recursively sort the first n-1 elements, then insert the last element into its correct position in that sorted prefix by shifting larger elements right. The base case is a range of length 0 or 1.

title: Quick Sorting
description: Given an array of integers, sort it in ascending order using quick sort. Pick a pivot (commonly the last element or a random index), partition the range so smaller elements sit left of the pivot and larger ones right, then recursively sort the two partitions. Average time complexity is O(n log n).

examples.explanation: With 3 as the first pivot, everything smaller moves left and everything larger moves right, then each side is sorted recursively.

title: Largest Element
description: Given an array of integers, find the largest element in it. Some variants ask for the index of the largest element instead of its value; if duplicates exist, the index of its last occurrence is usually expected. Aim for a single O(n) pass.

title: Second Largest Element
description: Given an array of integers, find the second largest distinct element. If it does not exist (all elements are equal or the array has fewer than two distinct values), return -1. Solve it in one pass without sorting the array.

examples.explanation: The distinct elements in order are 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, so the second largest is 5.

title: Check if the Array is Sorted II
description: Given an array of integers, determine whether it is sorted in non-decreasing order, i.e. every element is less than or equal to the one that follows it. Return true if sorted, otherwise false. A single pass with an early exit is enough.

examples.explanation: The drop from 3 to 1 violates the non-decreasing order.

title: Remove duplicates from Sorted array
description: Given a sorted array, remove the duplicates in place so that each unique element appears exactly once in the first k positions. Return k, the count of unique elements. The elements beyond the first k positions do not matter, and no extra array may be used.

examples.explanation: The unique elements 1, 2 and 3 occupy the first three positions.

title: Left Rotate Array by One
description: Given an array, rotate it left by exactly one position in place. Every element shifts one index down, and the first element wraps around to the end. Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Left Rotate Array by K Places
description: Given an array and an integer k, rotate the array left by k positions. For example, rotating [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] by 2 gives [3,4,5,6,7,1,2]. Handle k larger than n and do it in place with O(1) extra space using the reversal trick.

title: Move Zeros to End
description: Given an array of integers, move all zeros to the end while preserving the relative order of the non-zero elements. The rearrangement must be done in place, ideally in a single pass with O(1) extra space.

title: Linear Search
description: Given an array of integers and a target value, return the index of the first occurrence of the target using linear search. If the target is not present, return -1. A left-to-right scan is the expected approach.

title: Union of two sorted arrays
description: Given two sorted arrays, return their union as a sorted array containing every distinct element that appears in either array. If a value occurs in both arrays it must appear only once in the result. Use the two-pointer technique instead of a hash set.

examples.explanation: Common values 2 and 3 are kept once, and 6 is appended after exhausting arr1.

title: Find missing number
description: Given an array containing n distinct numbers taken from the range 0 to n, find the single missing number. The array is unsorted and exactly one value of the range is absent. The sum or XOR of 0..n gives an O(n) time, O(1) space solution.

examples.explanation: The range 0..3 is missing only 2.

title: Maximum Consecutive Ones
description: Given a binary array (only 0s and 1s), return the maximum number of consecutive 1s. Count the current run of ones and record its maximum whenever a zero resets the count. A single O(n) pass suffices.

examples.explanation: The longest run of consecutive ones has length 3 at the end.

title: Find the number that appears once, and other numbers twice.
description: Given an array where every element appears exactly twice except one element that appears once, find that single element. Solve it in linear time and constant space by XORing all elements together, since x XOR x = 0 cancels the pairs.

examples.explanation: 1 XOR 1 and 2 XOR 2 cancel out, leaving 4.

title: Longest subarray with given sum K(positives)
description: Given an array of positive integers and a target sum k, find the length of the longest subarray whose elements sum to exactly k. Use a prefix-sum hashmap storing the first index at which each sum appears, so each element is processed once.

examples.explanation: The subarray [2, 3, 5] sums to 10 and is the longest such window.

title: Longest subarray with sum K
description: Given an array that may contain positive integers, negative integers and zeros, find the length of the longest subarray with sum exactly k. Sliding window does not work with negatives, so use a hashmap of prefix sums to their earliest index.

examples.explanation: The subarray [1, -1, 5, -2] sums to 3 and has length 4.
The subarray [-1, 2] sums to 1.

title: Two Sum
description: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Exactly one valid answer exists and you may not use the same element twice. A hashmap of value to index finds the pair in O(n).

examples.explanation: 6 + 8 = 14, found at indices 1 and 3.

title: Sort an array of 0's 1's and 2's
description: Given an array containing only 0s, 1s and 2s, sort it in place without using any sorting algorithm. Use the Dutch National Flag algorithm with three pointers (low, mid, high) to arrange all 0s first, then 1s, then 2s in a single pass.

title: Majority Element-I
description: Given an array of size n, find the majority element, the value that appears more than n/2 times. It is guaranteed to exist. Boyer-Moore voting finds it in O(n) time and O(1) space.

examples.explanation: 2 appears 4 times out of 7, which is more than half.

title: Kadane's Algorithm
description: Given an array of integers (possibly negative), find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray. Kadane's algorithm tracks the best subarray ending at the current index and a running global maximum in one O(n) pass.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4, -1, 2, 1] has the largest sum 6.
With all elements negative, the best subarray is the single element -1.

title: Print subarray with maximum subarray sum (extended version of above problem)
description: Given an array of integers, print (or return) the subarray that has the maximum sum, extending Kadane's algorithm. Track the start index of the best run whenever a new maximum is found, so the winning subarray can be reconstructed.

examples.explanation: The maximum-sum subarray starts at index 3 and ends at index 6.

title: Stock Buy and Sell
description: You are given daily prices of a stock; buy on one day and sell on a later day to maximize profit. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profitable transaction exists. Track the minimum price so far and the best profit achievable today in one pass.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1 and sell at 6 for a profit of 5.
Prices only fall, so no transaction is made.

title: Rearrange array elements by sign
description: Given an array with an equal number of positive and negative integers, rearrange it so that positives and negatives alternate, starting with a positive, while keeping the relative order within each sign. For unequal counts, extras go to the end.

examples.explanation: Positives 3, 1, 2 and negatives -2, -5, -4 alternate in their original order.

title: Next Permutation
description: Given an array of digits representing a number, rearrange it into the next lexicographically greater permutation of those digits. If the arrangement is the largest possible, wrap around to the smallest. The replacement must be in place with constant extra memory.

examples.explanation: The pivot 1 is swapped with the next larger digit 3, then the suffix is reversed.
Already the largest permutation, so it wraps to the smallest.

title: Leaders in an Array
description: Given an array, an element is a leader if it is greater than or equal to every element to its right; the rightmost element is always a leader. Return all leaders in left-to-right order. A right-to-left scan keeping the running maximum gives O(n) time.

examples.explanation: 22 dominates everything after it, as do 12 and 6; 10 does not because of 22.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence in an Array
description: Given an unsorted array of integers, find the length of the longest sequence of consecutive elements (values differing by 1, regardless of position in the array). Solve it in O(n) by inserting everything into a hash set and starting counts only at sequence heads.

examples.explanation: The consecutive run 1, 2, 3, 4 has length 4.
The run 5, 6, 7, 8 has length 4.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description: Given an m x n matrix of integers, if an element is 0 set its entire row and column to zeros. The transformation must be done in place, ideally using the first row and first column as markers to achieve O(1) extra space.

examples.explanation: The single zero at (1,1) zeroes out row 1 and column 1.

title: Rotate matrix by 90 degrees
description: Given a square n x n matrix, rotate it by 90 degrees clockwise in place. The element at (i, j) moves to (j, n-1-i). The cleanest method is to transpose the matrix and then reverse every row.

title: Print the matrix in spiral manner
description: Given an m x n matrix, return all its elements in spiral order: traverse the top row left to right, the right column top to bottom, the bottom row right to left, and the left column bottom to top, then repeat on the remaining inner matrix.

title: Count subarrays with given sum
description: Given an array of integers and a target sum k, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose elements add up to exactly k. Use prefix sums with a hashmap that remembers how often each prefix sum has occurred, giving an O(n) solution.

examples.explanation: Subarrays [3, 1, 2] and [2, 4] both sum to 6.

title: Pascal's Triangle I
description: Given an integer numRows, return the first numRows rows of Pascal's triangle. Each row starts and ends with 1, and every interior entry is the sum of the two entries diagonally above it in the previous row.

title: Majority Element-II
description: Given an array of size n, return all elements that appear more than n/3 times. At most two such elements can exist, and the Boyer-Moore voting extension finds the candidates in O(n) time and O(1) space before a final verification pass.

examples.explanation: Both 1 and 2 appear 3 times out of 8, which exceeds 8/3.

title: 3 Sum
description: Given an array of n integers, find all unique triplets that sum to zero. The result must not contain duplicate triplets. Sort the array, fix each first element, then use two pointers on the remainder; skip duplicates at every step. Aim for O(n^2).

title: 4 Sum
description: Given an array of n integers and a target, return all unique quadruplets that sum to the target. Sort the array, fix the first two elements with nested loops, and finish each pair with two pointers, skipping duplicates throughout. Aim for O(n^3).

title: Largest Subarray with Sum 0
description: Given an array of integers that may be negative, find the length of the longest subarray whose sum is exactly 0. Track the earliest index of each prefix sum in a hashmap; a repeated prefix sum means the elements between form a zero-sum subarray.

examples.explanation: The subarray [-2, 2, -8, 1, 7] sums to 0 and has length 5.

title: Count subarrays with given xor K
description: Given an array of integers and a value k, count the subarrays whose XOR equals k. Use the prefix-XOR identity: a subarray (i, j] has XOR k exactly when prefixXor[j] XOR k equals prefixXor[i], so keep counts of seen prefix XORs in a hashmap.

examples.explanation: The subarrays [4, 2], [2, 2, 6], [6] and [4, 2, 2, 6, 4] all XOR to 6.

title: Merge Overlapping Subintervals
description: Given a list of intervals that may overlap, merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping result sorted by start. Sort by start time, then extend the current interval whenever the next one starts before or at its end.

examples.explanation: [1, 3] and [2, 6] overlap and merge into [1, 6].

title: Merge two sorted arrays without extra space
description: Given two sorted arrays arr1 (size n) and arr2 (size m), merge them so that the first n positions of arr1 and the last m positions of arr2 hold the fully sorted data, without using extra space. The gap or shell-sort style method achieves O((n+m) log(n+m)) with O(1) space.

title: Find the repeating and missing number
description: Given an unsorted array of n integers where each value from 1 to n appears exactly once except one number that repeats and one that is missing, find both the repeating and the missing number. Counting, math (sum and sum of squares) or XOR all work in O(n).

examples.explanation: 3 appears twice and 4 never appears among the values 1..5.

title: Count Inversions
description: Given an array, count the inversion pairs: pairs of indices (i, j) with i < j and arr[i] > arr[j]. Use a modified merge sort that counts cross inversions while merging, achieving O(n log n) instead of the brute-force O(n^2).

title: Reverse Pairs
description: Given an array, count the reverse pairs: index pairs (i, j) with i < j and arr[i] > 2 * arr[j]. Count them during merge sort by binary-searching the right half for each left element before merging, giving an O(n log n) solution.

examples.explanation: Pairs (4,1), (3,1) and (5,1) each satisfy arr[i] > 2 * arr[j].

title: Maximum Product Subarray in an Array
description: Given an array of integers, find the contiguous subarray with the largest product. Track both the maximum and minimum product ending at each index, because a negative number swaps them. Handle zeros by resetting the running products.

examples.explanation: The subarray [2, 3] has the largest product 6.
Any product touching a negative number here is beaten by the single 0.

title: Search X in sorted array
description: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target value, return the index of the target using binary search, or -1 if it is not present. Repeatedly halve the search range by comparing the target with the middle element, giving O(log n) time.

title: Lower Bound
description: Given a sorted array and a value x, return the lower bound: the smallest index i such that arr[i] >= x. If every element is smaller than x, return n (the array length). Implement it with binary search in O(log n).

examples.explanation: arr[3] = 15 is the first element greater than or equal to 9.

title: Upper Bound
description: Given a sorted array and a value x, return the upper bound: the smallest index i such that arr[i] > x (strictly greater). If no such element exists, return n. Implement it with binary search in O(log n).

examples.explanation: arr[2] = 6 is the first element strictly greater than 5.

title: Search insert position
description: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return the index where the target is found, or the index at which it would be inserted to keep the array sorted. This is exactly the lower bound of the target, solvable in O(log n).

examples.explanation: 6 is not present and would be inserted at index 3 between 4 and 7.

title: Floor and Ceil in Sorted Array
description: Given a sorted array and a value x, find the floor (the largest element <= x) and the ceil (the smallest element >= x) of x. Return -1 for either if it does not exist. Two binary searches solve this in O(log n).

title: First and last occurrence
description: Given a sorted array that may contain duplicates and a target, find the first and the last index of the target. Return [-1, -1] if the target is absent. Use lower-bound and upper-bound binary searches instead of a linear scan.

title: Count Occurrences in a Sorted Array
description: Given a sorted array with possible duplicates and a target, count how many times the target occurs. Find the first and last occurrence with binary search and take the difference, giving O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: 10 occupies indices 2, 3 and 4.

title: Search in rotated sorted array-I
description: Given an ascending array of distinct values that has been rotated between 1 and n times, find the index of a target value in O(log n). At every step, at least one half of the current range is fully sorted; check which half contains the target before recursing into it.

title: Search in rotated sorted array-II
description: Given a rotated sorted array that may contain duplicates, determine whether a target exists in it. Duplicates can make halves incomparable (arr[low] == arr[mid] == arr[high]); shrink the range by one in that case, giving O(log n) on average and O(n) worst case.

title: Find minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Given an ascending array of distinct values rotated between 1 and n times, return the minimum element in O(log n). The minimum is the only element smaller than its predecessor; binary search by comparing the middle against the right end.

title: Find out how many times the array is rotated
description: Given a sorted array that has been rotated, find how many times it was rotated (right rotations). The answer is the index of the minimum element, which binary search locates in O(log n); an unrotated array gives 0.

examples.explanation: The minimum element 1 sits at index 3, so the array was rotated 3 times.

title: Single element in a Sorted Array
description: Given a sorted array where every element appears exactly twice except one element that appears once, find the single element in O(log n). Before the single element, pairs start at even indices; after it, they start at odd indices; use this to guide the binary search.

title: Find peak element
description: Given an array where no two adjacent elements are equal, find any peak element: an index whose value is strictly greater than both neighbours (imagine arr[-1] and arr[n] as negative infinity). Binary search toward the larger neighbour converges on a peak in O(log n).

examples.explanation: 3 at index 2 is greater than both neighbours 2 and 1.

title: Find square root of a number
description: Given a non-negative integer n, return its integer square root, i.e. floor(sqrt(n)). Binary search the answer between 0 and n, or use the built-in power function; watch out for overflow when squaring mid.

title: Find Nth root of a number
description: Given two integers n and m, find the m-th root of n: an integer x such that x^m equals n. Return -1 if no integer root exists. Binary search x in [1, n] and compute powers with overflow-safe checks.

examples.explanation: No integer raised to the 4th power equals 69.

title: Koko eating bananas
description: Koko can eat at most k bananas per hour from one pile. Given the pile sizes and h hours, find the minimum integer eating speed k that lets her finish every pile within h hours. Binary search the speed; the feasibility check sums ceil(pile / k) over piles.

examples.explanation: At speed 4 the hours needed are 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8, which fits.

title: Minimum days to make M bouquets
description: A garden has n flowers that bloom on given days; a bouquet needs k adjacent bloomed flowers. Find the minimum number of days needed to make m bouquets. Binary search the day and check feasibility by scanning for runs of k adjacent bloomed flowers.

examples.explanation: Only on day 12 do two disjoint groups of 3 adjacent flowers bloom (indices 0-2 and 3-5).

title: Find the smallest divisor
description: Given an array of positive integers and a threshold, choose the smallest positive divisor so that the sum of ceil(arr[i] / divisor) is at most the threshold. Binary search the divisor; the sum decreases as the divisor grows.

examples.explanation: Divisor 5 gives 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5 <= 6, while divisor 4 gives 7 which exceeds it.

title: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days
description: Packages must be shipped in order over at most d days; each day a conveyor with capacity w ships a contiguous prefix of the remaining packages. Find the minimum capacity that satisfies the deadline. Binary search the capacity between max(weights) and sum(weights).

examples.explanation: Capacity 15 ships [1-5], [6-7], [8], [9], [10] in exactly 5 days; capacity 14 needs 6 days.

title: Kth Missing Positive Number
description: Given a strictly increasing array of positive integers and an integer k, return the k-th positive integer missing from the array. Either count missing numbers while scanning, or derive it with binary search on the count of missing values before each index.

examples.explanation: The missing numbers are 1, 5, 6, 8, 9, ... and the 5th one is 9.

title: Aggressive Cows
description: Given positions of n stalls and k aggressive cows, place the cows in stalls so the minimum distance between any two cows is as large as possible, and return that distance. Binary search the answer distance and greedily verify placements from the leftmost stall.

examples.explanation: Placing cows at stalls 0, 4, 7 and 10 keeps every pair at least 3 apart, and 4 is impossible.

title: Book Allocation Problem
description: Given pages of n books and m students, allocate a contiguous block of books to each student so the maximum pages any student reads is minimized; every student gets at least one book. Binary search the answer between the max single book and the total pages.

examples.explanation: Student 1 reads [12, 34, 67] and student 2 reads [90]; no split lowers the heavier load.

title: Split array - largest sum
description: Split an array of non-negative integers into at most k contiguous subarrays so that the largest subarray sum is minimized, and return that sum. Binary search the candidate sum between max(nums) and sum(nums), greedily counting the pieces needed.

examples.explanation: The split [7, 2, 5] and [10, 8] has maximum sum 18.

title: Painter's Partition
description: k painters take one unit of time per board and must each paint a contiguous set of boards. Given board lengths, find the minimum time in which the whole fence gets painted. It is the book allocation problem: binary search the maximum load per painter.

examples.explanation: Painter loads [5, 10], [30], [20, 15] cap the maximum at 35.

title: Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station
description: Given positions of existing gas stations on a line and an integer k, add k new stations anywhere so the maximum distance between adjacent stations is minimized. Binary search the answer distance with a high-precision feasibility check on how many stations each gap needs.

examples.explanation: Every unit gap receives one extra station, halving all gaps to 0.5.

title: Median of 2 sorted arrays
description: Given two sorted arrays of sizes n and m, return the median of all n + m elements in O(log(min(n, m))). Binary search the partition of the smaller array so the left halves contain exactly half the elements with every left value <= every right value.

examples.explanation: Merged order is [1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, 12, 15]; the middle elements 4 and 6 average to 5.

title: Kth element of 2 sorted arrays
description: Given two sorted arrays, find the k-th smallest element of their merged order without physically merging. Binary search how many elements to take from the smaller array, or run an O(k) two-pointer merge; the partition method gives O(log min(n, m)).

examples.explanation: The merged array is [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10] and its 5th element is 6.

title: Find row with maximum 1's
description: Given a boolean matrix where each row is sorted (all 0s before all 1s), find the row with the maximum number of 1s, returning the row index (or index and count). Count 1s per row in O(log n) by finding the first 1, or use the column index you are standing on.

title: Search in a 2D matrix
description: Given an m x n matrix where each row is sorted and the first integer of each row is greater than the last of the previous row, search for a target in O(log(m*n)). Treat the matrix as one flattened sorted array and binary search with index arithmetic (mid -> matrix[mid / n][mid % n]).

title: Search in 2D matrix - II
description: Given a matrix where every row and every column is sorted in ascending order, determine whether a target exists. Start at the top-right corner: move left when the value is too big and down when it is too small, eliminating a row or column each step in O(m + n).

title: Find Peak Element - II
description: A peak in a 2D matrix is a cell strictly greater than all four neighbours (out-of-bounds counts as -infinity); find the position of any peak. Binary search rows, take the column of the row maximum, and recurse into the larger vertical neighbour for O(m log n).

examples.explanation: 30 beats its neighbours 20, 14, 21 and 16.

title: Matrix Median
description: Given a matrix where each row is sorted, return the overall median of all n*m elements in less than O(n*m log(n*m)). Binary search the answer value using per-row upper-bound counts of elements <= mid.

examples.explanation: The 9 elements in order are [1, 2, 3, 3, 5, 6, 6, 9, 9] and the middle one is 5.

title: Remove Outermost Parentheses
description: Given a valid parentheses string, remove the outermost parentheses of every primitive substring and return the result. A primitive substring is a non-empty balanced piece that cannot be split further; track nesting depth with a counter instead of a stack.

examples.explanation: The primitives are '(()())' and '(())'; stripping their outer layers leaves '()()' and '()'.

title: Reverse words in a given string / Palindrome Check
description: Given a string of words separated by spaces, reverse the order of the words and return the new string, trimmed and joined by single spaces. The companion check asks whether a string reads the same after reversal; both can be solved in O(n).

examples.explanation: Leading and trailing spaces are dropped.

title: Largest Odd Number in a String
description: Given a string of digits representing a non-negative number, return the largest odd integer that is a contiguous leading substring (suffix-truncated) of it, or an empty string if no odd truncation exists. Since oddness depends only on the last digit, find the rightmost odd digit.

examples.explanation: 5 is odd while 52 is even, so truncate after the first digit.

title: Longest Common Prefix
description: Given an array of strings, return the longest common prefix shared by all of them, or the empty string if none exists. Compare characters column by column, or sort and compare only the first and last strings, in O(sum of lengths).

title: Isomorphic String
description: Given two strings of equal length, check whether they are isomorphic: characters in the first string can be replaced to obtain the second, with each character mapping to exactly one character and preserving order. Maintain two-way mappings to catch conflicts like 'badc' vs 'baba'.

examples.explanation: e -> a and g -> d consistently transform 'egg' into 'add'.

title: Rotate String
description: Given two strings s and goal of equal length, determine whether goal can be obtained by rotating s by some number of positions. A rotation of s is always a substring of s + s, so the check reduces to one containment test.

examples.explanation: Rotating 'abcde' left by 2 gives 'cdeab'.

title: Check if two strings are anagram of each other
description: Given two strings, check whether they are anagrams of each other: the same characters with exactly the same frequencies, order irrelevant. Compare sorted forms or count all 26 letter frequencies in O(n).

title: Sort Characters by Frequency
description: Given a string, sort its characters in decreasing order of frequency; characters with equal frequency may appear in any relative order. Bucket the characters by count and rebuild the string from the fullest buckets.

examples.explanation: 'e' appears twice, then 'r' and 't' once each.

title: Maximum Nesting Depth of the Parentheses
description: Given a balanced parentheses string possibly containing digits and operators, return its maximum nesting depth: the largest number of parentheses open at the same time. Scan once, increasing a counter on '(' and decreasing on ')'.

examples.explanation: Three parentheses are open simultaneously around the 8.

title: Roman to Integer
description: Given a Roman numeral string (letters I, V, X, L, C, D, M), convert it to its integer value. Walk left to right adding each symbol's value, but subtract the current value when a smaller symbol precedes a larger one, as in IV or XC.

examples.explanation: L = 50, V = 5 and III = 3.

title: String to Integer (atoi)
description: Implement atoi: parse a leading integer from a string after skipping whitespace and an optional sign, stopping at the first non-digit. Return 0 when no valid number exists and clamp the result to the 32-bit signed integer range [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].

examples.explanation: Parsing stops at 'c'.

title: Count Number of Substrings
description: Given a string of lowercase letters and an integer k, count the substrings that contain exactly k distinct characters. Use the sliding-window identity exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1) with a frequency map.

examples.explanation: The substrings 'ab', 'ba' and 'aba' each contain exactly two distinct letters.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
description: Given a string, return the longest palindromic substring. Expand around every possible center (2n - 1 of them: each character and each gap) and keep the longest expansion, in O(n^2) time and O(1) space.

examples.explanation: 'aba' is an equally long valid answer.

title: Sum of Beauty of All Substrings
description: The beauty of a string is the difference between the frequency of its most frequent and least frequent characters. Given a string, sum the beauty of every substring. Maintain per-substring frequency tables in O(n^2) since only 26 letters matter.

examples.explanation: The beauties of all substrings sum to 5, e.g. 'aab' has beauty 1 and 'bcb' has beauty 1.

title: Reverse every word in a string
description: Given a string of words, reverse the characters of every word in place while keeping the word order and spacing intact. Trim, split into words, reverse each with two pointers and rejoin, or do it fully in place with one reverse per segment.

title: Insertion at the head of Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list and an integer value, insert a new node with that value at the head (front) of the list and return the new head. The insertion must run in O(1) time by relinking one pointer.

title: Deletion of the head of LL
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, delete the head node and return the new head of the remaining list. Handle the empty list by returning null; the deletion itself is a single pointer relink in O(1).

title: Find the length of the Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the number of nodes it contains. Walk from head to null counting one node per step, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Search in Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list and a target value, determine whether the value exists in the list (returning its 1-based position or true/false as the variant asks). Traverse node by node, stopping early on a match.

title: Insert node before head in Doubly Linked List
description: Given the head of a doubly linked list and a value, insert a new node with that value before the current head, wiring both next and prev pointers correctly, and return the new head. The insertion is O(1).

title: Delete head of Doubly Linked List
description: Given the head of a doubly linked list, delete the head node and return the new head, taking care to null the prev pointer of the surviving first node. Handle the empty and single-node cases explicitly.

title: Reverse a Doubly Linked List
description: Given the head of a doubly linked list, reverse it in place so the last node becomes the head. Swap the next and prev pointers of every node during one traversal; both the iterative and recursive forms run in O(n) with O(1) extra space (iterative).

title: Middle of a LinkedList [TortoiseHare Method]
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return its middle node. Use the tortoise-and-hare technique: slow moves one step, fast moves two, and slow is at the middle when fast reaches the end. For an even number of nodes, the second middle is returned.

title: Reverse a LinkedList [Iterative]
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse it iteratively in place using three pointers (prev, curr, next) so that the last node becomes the head. The reversal runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

title: Reverse a LL
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse it using recursion: reverse the sublist after the current node, then attach the current node to its end. Each call handles one pointer relink, giving O(n) time and O(n) recursion stack.

title: Detect a loop in LL
description: Given the head of a linked list that may contain a cycle (a node's next pointer pointing back to an earlier node), detect whether a cycle exists. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm moves a slow and a fast pointer and detects a cycle if they meet, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

examples.input: list = 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, node 5 links back to node 3

title: Find the starting point in LL
description: Given a linked list with a cycle, return the node where the cycle begins. After Floyd's slow and fast pointers meet inside the cycle, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet exactly at the cycle's entry.

title: Length of loop in LL
description: Given a linked list with a cycle, return the number of nodes in the cycle. Find any node inside the loop with Floyd's algorithm, then walk once around until you return to it, counting the steps.

examples.input: list = 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, node 5 links back to node 3
examples.explanation: The cycle is 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 3.

title: Check if LL is palindrome or not
description: Given the head of a singly linked list of integers, check whether the sequence of values reads the same forwards and backwards. Reverse the second half in place after finding the middle, or copy values to an array, achieving O(n) time.

title: Segregate odd and even nodes in Linked List
description: Given the head of a linked list, rearrange it so all odd-valued nodes come before even-valued nodes while preserving the relative order within each group. Stitch separate odd and even chains and join them, in one O(n) pass.

title: Remove Nth node from the back of the LL
description: Given the head of a linked list and an integer n, remove the n-th node from the end in one pass. Use a fast pointer that starts n steps ahead; when it reaches the end, the slow pointer sits just before the node to delete.

title: Delete the middle node in LL
description: Given the head of a linked list, delete its middle node: the second of the two middles for an even length, and nothing for a list of one node. A slow pointer that lags one step behind the classic tortoise lands right before the middle.

title: Sort LL
description: Given the head of a linked list, sort it in O(n log n) time and O(1) space where possible. Merge sort is the natural fit: find the middle with tortoise-and-hare, recursively sort both halves, and merge the sorted runs.

title: Sort a Linked List of 0's 1's and 2's
description: Given the head of a linked list containing only 0s, 1s and 2s, sort it in one pass without changing node values if possible. Maintain three dummy chains for 0s, 1s and 2s, then link them together.

title: Find the intersection point of Y LL
description: Given the heads of two linked lists that merge into a common tail (a Y shape), return the node where they intersect; the tails after that node are identical. Align both pointers to the same distance from the end by swapping lists at the null, in O(n) and O(1) space.

examples.explanation: Both lists share the tail starting at 8.

title: Add one to a number represented by LL
description: A number is stored in a linked list, one digit per node, most significant digit first. Add one to the number and return the resulting list, correctly handling carries that ripple left (for example 199 becomes 200) and new leading digits (999 becomes 1000).

title: Add two numbers in Linked List
description: Two non-negative numbers are stored in linked lists with digits in reverse order (least significant first). Add them and return the sum as a similarly stored list, carrying as you walk both lists in one O(max(m, n)) pass.

title: Delete all occurrences of a key in DLL
description: Given the head of a doubly linked list and a key, delete every node whose value equals the key, correctly rewiring prev and next pointers (including the head) for each deletion. One traversal suffices; return the resulting head.

title: Find Pairs with Given Sum in Doubly Linked List
description: Given a sorted doubly linked list and a target sum, find all pairs of nodes whose values add up to the target. Start a pointer at each end and move inward based on the comparison, yielding O(n) time after O(n) traversal to reach the tail.

examples.explanation: Both pairs sum to 7 and no others do.

title: Remove duplicates from sorted DLL
description: Given a sorted doubly linked list, remove duplicate values so each value appears exactly once, keeping the first occurrence of each. Rewire prev and next pointers around every removed node and return the head.

title: Reverse LL in group of given size K
description: Given the head of a linked list and an integer k, reverse the nodes of the list k at a time and return the modified list; a final incomplete group of fewer than k nodes stays as is. Recursively reverse each group while preserving the links between groups.

examples.explanation: The first three nodes reverse; the leftover pair of two nodes is untouched.

title: Rotate a LL
description: Given the head of a linked list and an integer k, rotate the list to the right by k places. Make the list circular, compute the effective rotation modulo the length, break the circle at the correct node and return the new head, in O(n).

title: Flattening of LL
description: Given a linked list where each node has a next pointer to the main row and a bottom pointer to a vertical chain (each vertical chain is sorted, as is the main row), flatten the structure into one singly linked list sorted by value, connected through bottom pointers.

title: Clone a LL with random and next pointer
description: Given the head of a linked list where each node has a next pointer and a random pointer to any node or null, build a deep copy of the list with identical next and random structure. The O(1)-space trick interleaves copied nodes into the original list before extracting them.

examples.output: a brand new list of five nodes with the same values and random targets

title: Recursive Implementation of atoi()
description: Implement string-to-integer conversion recursively: skip leading spaces and an optional sign, then convert digits one by one through recursive calls. Follow atoi rules including clamping to the 32-bit signed range and stopping at the first non-digit.

title: Pow(x, n)
description: Implement pow(x, n): raise x to the integer power n in O(log n) using fast exponentiation - halve the exponent each step and square the half-result, negating once for negative exponents. Handle overflow by using a 64-bit exponent.

title: Count Good Numbers
description: A good number is a digit string of length n where digits at even indices (0-based) are even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) and digits at odd indices are prime (2, 3, 5, 7). Count good numbers of length n, modulo 10^9 + 7, using fast exponentiation of 5 and 4.

examples.explanation: The single digit must be even: 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
5 * 4 * 5 * 4 = 400 combinations.

title: Sort a stack using recursion
description: Given a stack of integers, sort it (smallest on top, or largest on top as specified) using only recursion - no loops or extra data structures besides the call stack. The pattern is: pop the top, recursively sort the rest, then insert the popped value back in sorted position.

title: Reverse a Stack
description: Given a stack, reverse its elements using only recursion (the call stack is the only auxiliary storage). Pop the top, recursively reverse the remainder, then push the popped element to the bottom of the reversed stack.

title: Generate Binary Strings Without Consecutive 1s
description: Generate all binary strings of length n that contain no two consecutive 1s. Recurse on the next character, remembering that a '1' may only follow a '0'; print or collect every complete string.

examples.explanation: 11 is excluded because it has consecutive ones.

title: Generate Parentheses
description: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all strings of well-formed parentheses of length 2n. Recurse with counts of open and close brackets used, only adding '(' when opens remain and ')' when it would not unbalance the prefix.

examples.explanation: All five distinct valid combinations.

title: Power Set
description: Given an array of distinct integers, return the power set: every possible subset including the empty set and the full set (2^n subsets). Either decide include-or-skip for each element recursively, or index subsets by bitmask.

title: Count all subsequences with sum K
description: Given an array of integers and a target k, count all subsequences (elements in original order, not necessarily contiguous) whose elements sum to exactly k. Recurse with pick/not-pick choices, optionally pruning when all values are positive.

examples.explanation: The subsequences [2] and [1, 1] sum to 2.

title: Check if there exists a subsequence with sum K
description: Given an array of non-negative integers and a target k, determine whether any subsequence sums to exactly k. Recurse with pick/not-pick and return true as soon as a matching branch is found; the empty subsequence counts only for k = 0.

examples.explanation: The subsequence [2, 3] sums to 5.

title: Combination Sum
description: Given an array of distinct candidates and a target, return all unique combinations summing to the target where each candidate may be reused any number of times. Recurse on the same index after picking to allow reuse; combinations are printed in non-decreasing order.

title: Combination Sum II
description: Given an array of candidates (may contain duplicates) and a target, return all unique combinations summing to the target where each candidate is used at most once. Sort first, recurse on the next index, and skip duplicate values at the same recursion depth.

title: Subsets I
description: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set). Build them recursively by deciding for each element whether to include it, yielding 2^n subsets that may be in any order.

title: Subsets II
description: Given an integer array that may contain duplicates, return all unique subsets (the power set without repeated subsets). Sort the array and skip equal elements at the same recursion level so no subset is generated twice.

title: Combination Sum III
description: Find all valid combinations of k distinct digits from 1 to 9 that sum to n, each digit used at most once. Recurse over the digits 1..9, tracking how many slots remain and how much sum is left.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
description: Given a string of digits (2-9), return all possible letter combinations the number could represent on a phone keypad (2 = abc, 3 = def, ...). Explore every mapping of each digit in order; the result has product-of-mapping-sizes entries.

examples.output: ad, ae, af, bd, be, bf, cd, ce, cf

title: Palindrome partitioning
description: Given a string s, partition it into substrings such that every piece is a palindrome; return all possible partitions. Recurse on every prefix that is a palindrome and collect complete partitionings at the end of the string.

title: Word Search
description: Given an m x n grid of letters and a word, determine whether the word can be traced as a path of adjacent cells (up, down, left, right), using each cell at most once. Backtrack from every cell that starts the word, marking visited cells during the recursion.

examples.explanation: The B can only be reused, which is not allowed.

title: N Queen
description: Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so no two queens attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal), and return all distinct boards. Backtrack row by row, using sets or arrays to check column and diagonal conflicts in O(1).

examples.explanation: One board places queens in row 1, 3, 0, 2 across rows 0-3 ('.Q..', '...Q', 'Q...', '..Q.').

title: Rat in a Maze
description: Given an n x n binary maze where 1 is an open cell and 0 is blocked, list all paths from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell moving only right or down (as the classic variant states), returning them in lexicographic order of direction letters (D, L, R, U).

examples.explanation: Both paths avoid the blocked cells and end at (3,3).

title: Word Break
description: Given a string s and a dictionary of words, determine whether s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words. Try every dictionary word that matches a prefix and recurse on the remainder (memoize for efficiency).

title: M Coloring Problem
description: Given an undirected graph and m colors, determine whether the vertices can be colored so no two adjacent vertices share a color. Backtrack vertex by vertex, trying each color that conflicts with none of its already-colored neighbours.

title: Sudoku Solver
description: Given a 9 x 9 Sudoku board partially filled with digits 1-9 (empty cells marked '.'), fill every cell so each row, column and 3 x 3 box contains all nine digits. Backtrack over empty cells, trying digits that violate no constraint.

title: Expression Add Operators
description: Given a string of digits num and an integer target, return all expressions formed by inserting the binary operators '+', '-' or '*' between digits that evaluate to the target. Backtrack over operator choices and operand boundaries, tracking the running value and the last term for multiplication precedence.

title: Check if the i-th bit is Set or Not
description: Given an integer n and a bit position i (0-based from the least significant bit), determine whether the i-th bit of n is set to 1. Check it with a single AND against a mask: (n >> i) & 1, or n & (1 << i).

examples.explanation: Bit 2 of 1101 is 1.

title: Check if a Number is Odd or Not
description: Given an integer n, determine whether it is odd or even using bit operations only. The least significant bit encodes parity directly: n & 1 is 1 exactly when n is odd.

examples.explanation: 5 in binary is 101 and its last bit is 1.

title: Check if a Number is Power of 2 or Not
description: Given an integer n, check whether it is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, ...). A positive power of two has exactly one set bit, so the check n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0 works in O(1).

examples.explanation: 16 is 10000 in binary with a single set bit.

title: Count the Number of Set Bits
description: Given an unsigned integer n, count the number of set bits (1s) in its binary representation. Brian Kernighan's trick n &= (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit each iteration, running once per set bit; a loop over all bits also works.

examples.explanation: 13 is 1101 in binary, containing three 1s.

title: Set/Unset the rightmost unset bit
description: Given an integer n, set its rightmost unset bit (the lowest 0 bit) to 1 and return the result; if every bit is set, return n unchanged. Setting the rightmost unset bit of n is equivalent to computing n | (n + 1).

examples.explanation: The rightmost unset bit is bit 0; setting it yields 111.

title: Swap Two Numbers
description: Given two integers a and b, swap their values without using a temporary variable, using only the XOR operation. Apply the sequence a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b, exploiting the fact that x ^ x = 0 and XOR is self-inverse.

title: Divide two numbers without multiplication and division
description: Given two integers dividend and divisor, compute the truncated quotient without using multiplication, division or the modulo operator. Repeatedly subtract the largest divisor << k that fits, accumulating 1 << k into the quotient; clamp results to the 32-bit signed range.

examples.explanation: Truncation toward zero turns -3.5 into -3.

title: Minimum Bit Flips to Convert Number
description: Given two integers start and goal, return the minimum number of bit flips needed to convert start into goal. XOR the two numbers to mark every differing bit, then count the set bits of the result.

examples.explanation: The XOR 1101 has three set bits.

title: Single Number - I
description: Given an array where every element appears exactly twice except one element that appears once, find that single number in linear time and constant space. XOR all elements: pairs cancel to 0 and the unique value survives.

title: Power Set Bit Manipulation
description: Given an array of integers, generate its power set using bit manipulation: iterate a mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 and include arr[i] in a subset whenever bit i of the mask is set. All 2^n subsets appear in mask order.

title: XOR of numbers in a given range
description: Given an integer n, compute the XOR of all numbers from 0 to n (i.e. 0 ^ 1 ^ 2 ^ ... ^ n). The pattern repeats every four values: n % 4 == 0 gives n, 1 gives 1, 2 gives n + 1, and 3 gives 0, so the answer is O(1).

title: Single Number - III
description: Given an array where every element appears exactly twice except two elements that appear once each, find both unique numbers in linear time and constant space. XOR everything to get a ^ b, isolate the lowest set bit (a differing bit), and partition the array by that bit.

examples.explanation: 3 and 5 appear once; all other values pair up.

title: Print Prime Factors of a Number
description: Given an integer n, print all of its prime factors with multiplicity in increasing order. Divide out each prime repeatedly starting from 2; a factor needs checking only up to sqrt(n), giving O(sqrt n) time.

title: Divisors of a Number
description: Given an integer n, print all its divisors (factors) in increasing order. Iterate candidate divisors up to sqrt(n), recording both d and n / d when d divides n, then sort the collected pairs for increasing output.

title: Count primes in range L to R
description: Given a range [L, R], count how many primes lie in it (a prime is an integer greater than 1 divisible only by 1 and itself). Build a Sieve of Eratosthenes once up to R and answer queries by prefix-summing the sieve, or answer a single range directly.

examples.explanation: The primes are 2, 3, 5 and 7.
The primes are 11, 13, 17 and 19.

title: Prime factorisation of a Number
description: Given an integer n, express it as a product of prime powers, for example 60 = 2^2 * 3^1 * 5^1. Trial-divide by each prime factor, counting how many times it divides n, and print each prime with its exponent.

title: Pow(x,n)
description: Implement pow(x, n) using bit manipulation: process the exponent bit by bit, squaring the base for every bit and multiplying the answer when the bit is set. This binary exponentiation runs in O(log n) with no recursion.

examples.explanation: 10 is 1010 in binary, so the answer multiplies in x^8 and x^2.

title: Implement Stack using Arrays
description: Implement a stack (LIFO) backed by a plain array with the operations push(x), pop(), top() and size(), each in O(1). Guard against popping or peeking an empty stack with an underflow message or exception.

examples.input: push(2), push(3), push(4), pop(), push(5), top()

title: Implement Queue using Arrays
description: Implement a queue (FIFO) backed by a plain array with the operations push/enqueue(x), pop/dequeue(), front() and size(), each in O(1). Use a head index that advances on dequeue so elements need not be shifted; guard against underflow.

examples.input: enqueue(2), enqueue(3), enqueue(4), dequeue(), enqueue(5), front()

title: Implement Stack using Queue
description: Implement a stack using one or two queues so push, pop, top and size all behave like a LIFO stack. With a single queue, push rotates the queue after insertion; with two queues, push empties the main queue into a helper to bring the new element to the front.

title: Implement Queue using Stack
description: Implement a queue using two stacks so enqueue and dequeue follow FIFO order. Push onto an input stack for enqueue; for dequeue, pour the input stack into an output stack once when it is empty, then pop from the output stack (each element is moved at most once).

title: Implement stack using Linkedlist
description: Implement a stack backed by a singly linked list with O(1) push, pop, top and size by operating at the head. Pushing inserts a new head node; popping removes the head and returns its value, with an underflow check for the empty stack.

title: Implement queue using Linkedlist
description: Implement a queue backed by a singly linked list with O(1) enqueue and dequeue by keeping both head and tail pointers. Enqueue appends at the tail; dequeue removes the head, handling the empty-queue and last-node cases.

title: Balanced Paranthesis
description: Given a string containing only the characters '()', '[]' and '{}', determine whether the brackets are balanced: every opening bracket must close in the correct order with the matching type. Push openings onto a stack and match closings against the top in O(n).

examples.explanation: ']' arrives before the pending '(' is closed.

title: Implement Min Stack
description: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top and retrieving the minimum element, every operation in O(1) time. Store the running minimum alongside each value (or keep a second min-stack updated on push and pop).

examples.input: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin(), pop(), top(), getMin()

title: Infix to Postfix Conversion
description: Given an infix expression containing letters, digits and the operators +, -, *, /, ^ and parentheses, convert it to postfix (Reverse Polish) notation using a stack. Higher-precedence operators (and left parentheses) stack up and pop when a lower-precedence operator or closing parenthesis arrives.

examples.explanation: Multiplication binds tighter, so it is emitted first.

title: Prefix to Infix Conversion
description: Given a prefix expression (operator before operands), convert it into a fully parenthesized infix expression by scanning right to left. Push operands on a stack; on an operator, pop two operands and push the string '(' + a + op + b + ')'.

title: Prefix to Postfix Conversion
description: Given a prefix expression, convert it directly to postfix notation. Scan right to left with a stack: operands push, and an operator pops two strings and pushes a + b + operator.

title: Postfix to Prefix Conversion
description: Given a postfix expression, convert it to prefix notation. Scan left to right with a stack: operands push, and an operator pops two strings and pushes operator + a + b.

examples.explanation: (A+B) * (C-D) becomes '*' applied to '+AB' and '-CD'.

title: Postfix to Infix Conversion
description: Given a postfix expression, convert it to a fully parenthesized infix expression. Scan left to right with a stack: operands push, and an operator pops two strings and pushes '(' + a + operator + b + ')'.

title: Infix to Prefix Conversion
description: Given an infix expression, convert it to prefix notation. Reverse the string (swapping bracket directions), run the infix-to-postfix conversion with mirrored associativity, then reverse the result so every operator precedes its operands.

examples.explanation: y*z/w binds first, then the additions left to right.

title: Next Greater Element
description: Given an array, find the next greater element to the right for every position: the nearest following element that is strictly larger, or -1 when none exists. Use a monotonic decreasing stack of indices, popping when a bigger value arrives, in O(n).

title: Next Greater Element - 2
description: Given a circular array, find each element's next greater element, wrapping around the end of the array to search the beginning; use -1 when no greater value exists. Iterate the doubled array with a monotonic stack of indices modulo n.

examples.explanation: The last 1 finds the greater 2 by wrapping to the start.

title: Next Smaller Element
description: Given an array, find the next smaller element to the right for every position: the nearest following element that is strictly smaller, or -1 when none exists. Use a monotonic increasing stack of indices, popping when a smaller value arrives, in O(n).

title: Number of Greater Elements to the Right
description: Given an array, count for every element how many elements to its right are strictly greater. The brute force is O(n^2); smarter versions use a sorted container or merge-sort-style counting while scanning from the right.

examples.explanation: For 1, the elements 2, 3 and 4 all lie to its right and are greater.

title: Trapping Rainwater
description: Given a non-negative elevation map where each bar has width 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining. Each position holds water up to min(max height to its left, max height to its right) minus its own height; two pointers compute it in O(n) with O(1) space.

title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
description: Given an array of positive integers, sum the minimum of every contiguous subarray, modulo 10^9 + 7. For each element, count the subarrays in which it is the minimum (distance to the previous smaller and next smaller-or-equal elements) using a monotonic stack, in O(n).

examples.explanation: Subarray minimums are 3+1+2+4+1+1+2+1+1+1 = 17.

title: Asteroid Collision
description: Given an array of asteroids with positive values moving right and negative values moving left at equal speed, simulate collisions: moving-apart asteroids never meet, while meeting ones destroy each other based on absolute size until stable. Return the final state using a stack.

examples.explanation: 10 destroys the smaller -5.
-5 destroys 2, then explodes against 10.

title: Sum of Subarray Ranges
description: Given an integer array, sum the range (maximum minus minimum) of every contiguous subarray. Reuse the monotonic-stack technique: total = sum of all subarray maximums minus sum of all subarray minimums, each computed in O(n).

examples.explanation: The ranges are 0, 0, 0, 1, 1 and 2, summing to 4.

title: Remove K Digits
description: Given a numeric string num and an integer k, remove k digits so the remaining number (with leading zeros stripped) is as small as possible; return the empty string if everything is removed. Greedily pop larger digits off a stack while removals remain.

examples.explanation: Removing 4, 3 and 2 leaves the smallest arrangement.

title: Largest rectangle in a histogram
description: Given an array of bar heights representing a histogram where each bar has width 1, find the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the histogram. Use a monotonic increasing stack of indices; on each pop, the popped height times the popped width bounds a candidate rectangle.

examples.explanation: Bars 5 and 6 form a 2 x 5 rectangle of area 10.

title: Maximum Rectangles
description: Given a binary matrix of 0s and 1s, find the area of the largest rectangle containing only 1s. Treat each row as the base of a histogram (heights = consecutive 1s above, resetting at 0s) and apply the largest-rectangle-in-histogram stack per row, in O(n*m).

examples.explanation: A 2 x 3 block of 1s sits in rows 1-2, columns 2-4.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Given an array of integers and a window size k, return the maximum of every contiguous window of length k as the window slides from left to right. A deque of indices keeps candidates in decreasing order so each element enters and leaves once, giving O(n).

title: Stock span problem
description: The span of a stock's price on day i is the maximum number of consecutive days (ending today) over which the price has been less than or equal to today's price. Compute the span for every day using a stack of previous greater elements, in O(n).

examples.explanation: On the last day the prices 80, 60, 70, 60 and 75 are all <= 85, giving a span of six days.

title: Celebrity Problem
description: In a party of n people, a celebrity is known by everyone else but knows nobody; given the n x n 'knows' matrix, find the celebrity or return -1. A two-pointer elimination (or a stack) discards one non-celebrity per comparison, finishing with at most one candidate to verify in O(n).

examples.explanation: Everyone knows person 1, and person 1 knows nobody.

title: LRU Cache
description: Design a fixed-capacity LRU cache supporting get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1): evicting the least recently used entry when full. Combine a hashmap from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency, moving nodes to the front on every access.

examples.input: capacity = 2, put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2)
examples.explanation: Adding key 3 evicts key 2, the least recently used.

title: LFU Cache
description: Design a fixed-capacity LFU cache supporting get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1), evicting the least frequently used entry (most recent among ties) when full. Bucket keys by frequency with doubly linked lists plus a hashmap, promoting a key to the next bucket on every access.

examples.input: capacity = 2, put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2)
examples.explanation: Key 1 was touched once so key 2 becomes the least frequently used and is evicted.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. Slide a window with a hashmap of each character's last seen index, moving the left bound past duplicates, in O(n).

examples.explanation: The longest substring without repeats is 'abc'.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
description: Given a binary array and an integer k, find the longest contiguous subarray of 1s achievable if you may flip at most k zeros. Slide a window that never holds more than k zeros, tracking the best length, in O(n).

examples.explanation: Flipping the two zeros next to the run of four 1s gives six consecutive 1s.

title: Fruit Into Baskets
description: Two baskets each hold one fruit type; walking a row of fruit trees you must pick one fruit from every tree starting at some tree until you hit a third type. Find the maximum number of trees you can pick from - the longest subarray with at most 2 distinct values.

examples.explanation: Picking [2, 3, 2, 2] uses only fruit types 2 and 3.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description: Given a string of uppercase letters and an integer k, find the length of the longest substring you can turn into a run of one repeating character by changing at most k characters. Slide a window that keeps (window length - count of the most frequent letter) <= k.

examples.explanation: Replacing one 'A' in 'ABBA' yields 'BBBB'.

title: Binary Subarrays With Sum
description: Given a binary array, count the subarrays that sum to exactly goal. Since zeros make prefix sums repeat, use a hashmap of prefix-sum counts (atMost(goal) - atMost(goal - 1) also works), giving O(n).

examples.explanation: The subarrays [1,0,1], [1,0,1,0], [0,1,0,1] and [1,0,1] at the end sum to 2.

title: Count number of Nice subarrays
description: Given an array of integers, count the number of 'nice' subarrays: subarrays containing exactly k odd numbers. Convert each element to its parity and count subarrays with exactly k ones, using prefix sums or the atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) trick.

examples.explanation: The subarrays [1, 1, 2, 1] and [1, 2, 1, 1] each contain exactly three odd numbers.

title: Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters
description: Given a string consisting only of the characters a, b and c, count the substrings that contain at least one of each. For every right endpoint, find the smallest valid left bound and add its index + 1 to the answer, or use atMost(3) - atMost(2).

examples.explanation: Every substring of length >= 3 except 'bca'-style misses contains all three; ten substrings qualify.

title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards
description: Cards are laid out in a row; you must take exactly k cards from the beginning or the end (in any order) to maximize the total points collected. Equivalently, drop a contiguous middle block of n - k cards with the minimum sum; try every split with prefix sums.

examples.explanation: Taking cards 1, 6 and 5 from the ends collects 12 points.

title: Longest Substring With At Most K Distinct Characters
description: Given a string and an integer k, find the length of the longest substring containing at most k distinct characters. Slide a window with a frequency map, shrinking from the left whenever the distinct count exceeds k, in O(n).

examples.explanation: The substring 'aaabbb' uses only two distinct characters and has length 6.

title: Subarrays with K Different Integers
description: Given an array of positive integers, count the subarrays with exactly k different values. Exactly-k equals (subarrays with at most k) minus (subarrays with at most k-1); each atMost count comes from a sliding window with a frequency map.

examples.explanation: Seven subarrays contain exactly two distinct values, such as [1,2], [2,1] and [1,2,1,2].

title: Minimum Window Substring
description: Given strings s and t, return the minimum window substring of s that contains every character of t (with multiplicity), or the empty string if none exists. Expand a window until it covers t, then contract from the left while it still covers, in O(n).

examples.explanation: 'BANC' is the shortest substring of s containing A, B and C.

title: Minimum Window Subsequence
description: Given strings s1 and s2, find the minimum-length substring of s1 in which s2 appears as a subsequence; return the empty string if no such window exists. Slide a two-pointer subsequence match and walk the window back to find its smallest valid start.

examples.explanation: 'bcde' contains b, then d, then e in order and is the shortest such window.

title: Kth smallest element in an array [use priority queue]
description: Given an unsorted array of integers and an integer k, return the k-th smallest element. Maintain a max-heap of size k while scanning (or a min-heap of all elements), so the answer surfaces in O(n log k) time.

examples.explanation: Sorted order is 3, 4, 7, 10, 15, 20 and the third smallest is 7.

title: Implement Min Heap
description: Implement a min-heap from scratch with insert(value), getMin() and extractMin() operations, each running in O(log n). Maintain the heap property with sift-up on insert and sift-down on extract, keeping the minimum at index 0 of the array.

examples.input: insert(5), insert(3), insert(8), insert(1), extractMin(), getMin()

title: Check if an array represents a min heap
description: Given an array, determine whether it represents a valid min-heap: for every index i, arr[i] must be less than or equal to arr[2i+1] and arr[2i+2] whenever those children exist. A single bottom-up check of every internal node decides it in O(n).

examples.explanation: The parent 5 is greater than its child 2.

title: Convert Min Heap to Max Heap
description: Given an array that forms a min-heap, convert it in place into a max-heap in O(n). Run the standard bottom-up heapify (sift-down from the last internal node to the root) using the greater-than comparison instead of building it top down, which would cost O(n log n).

title: K-th Largest element in an array
description: Given an unsorted array and an integer k, return the k-th largest element. Keep a min-heap of size k while scanning so the heap root always holds the k-th largest seen so far, finishing in O(n log k).

examples.explanation: Sorted descending the array is 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, so the second largest is 5.

title: Sort K sorted array
description: Given a nearly sorted array where every element is at most k positions away from its sorted position, sort it efficiently in O(n log k) using a min-heap. Push the first k+1 elements, then repeatedly pop the minimum and push the next element.

title: Merge K sorted Lists
description: Given k sorted linked lists (or arrays), merge them all into one sorted result. Push the head of every list into a min-heap, repeatedly extract the smallest node and push its successor, producing O(N log k) where N is the total number of nodes.

title: Replace Elements by Their Rank
description: Given an array of distinct integers, replace every element with its rank: 1 for the smallest, 2 for the next, and so on. Sort a copy (or use a hashmap keyed by sorted position) and map each value to its 1-based rank.

title: Task Scheduler
description: Given a task list (uppercase letters) and a cooldown n, tasks of the same type must be separated by at least n seconds of other work or idle time. Compute the minimum total time to finish all tasks using frequency buckets or a max-heap with a cooldown queue.

examples.input: tasks = [A, A, A, B, B, B], n = 2
examples.explanation: A B idle A B idle A B fits the cooldown in 8 slots.

title: Hand of Straights
description: Given an array hand of card values and an integer groupSize, determine whether the cards can be rearranged into groups of groupSize consecutive cards. Greedily consume the smallest remaining card and its successors using a TreeMap or counters.

examples.explanation: The cards split into groups [1,2,3], [2,3,4] and [6,7,8].

title: Design Twitter
description: Design a simplified Twitter supporting postTweet(userId, tweetId), getNewsFeed(userId) returning the 10 most recent tweets of the user and their followees, follow/unfollow, all efficiently. Keep per-user tweet lists with global timestamps and merge feeds with a heap.

examples.input: user1 posts tweets 5 then 3, user1 follows user2 who posted tweet 10, getNewsFeed(1)
examples.explanation: The feed shows tweets newest first from both the user and the followee.

title: Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks
description: Given sticks of various lengths, joining two sticks of lengths a and b costs a + b; combine all sticks into one with minimum total cost. Always join the two shortest sticks (min-heap), like Huffman merging, in O(n log n).

examples.explanation: Join 2+3 for 5, then 5+4 for 9, totalling 14.

title: Kth largest element in a stream of running integers
description: Design a class that receives a running stream of integers and, after each add, returns the k-th largest element seen so far. Keep a min-heap of size k so the root is always the answer, with O(log k) per addition.

examples.input: k = 3, stream starts [4, 5, 8, 2], then add(3), add(5), add(10)
examples.explanation: After adding 3 the third largest of {2,3,4,5,8} is 4, and so on.

title: Maximum Sum Combination
description: Given two arrays a and b of equal size, a sum combination is a[i] + b[j]; return the k largest sum combinations. Start from the pair of the two largest elements in a max-heap and expand neighbours (i+1, j) and (i, j+1), avoiding duplicates with a visited set.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
description: Design a data structure that accepts a stream of integers and returns the median of all inserted values in O(log n) per operation. Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, rebalancing so their sizes differ by at most one.

examples.output: median 5 after two adds, then 4.0, then 4.0
examples.explanation: Sorted values after all inserts are [1, 3, 5, 15] with median 4.0.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
description: Given an integer array and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements; ties may be broken arbitrarily. Bucket values by frequency (frequency <= n) or use a heap of (count, value) pairs, achieving O(n log k) or better.

title: Assign Cookies
description: Given greed factors of children and sizes of cookies, a child is content only when a cookie size is at least their greed; each child gets at most one cookie. Maximize the number of content children by greedily feeding the least greedy child with the smallest sufficient cookie.

examples.explanation: Only one cookie is big enough for the least greedy child.

title: Fractional Knapsack
description: Given item values, item weights and a knapsack capacity where items can be broken into fractions, maximize the total value carried. Sort items by value-per-unit-weight descending and greedily fill the bag, taking fractions of the last item if needed.

examples.explanation: Take the first two items fully (160) plus two-thirds of the third (80).

title: Lemonade Change
description: You sell lemonade at 5 a unit and customers pay with 5, 10 or 20 bills in order; you start with no change. Determine whether you can provide exact change to every customer, greedily preferring to give a 10 bill back for 20 payments.

examples.explanation: The third 20 is changed with one 10 and one 5.

title: Valid Paranthesis Checker
description: Given a string of '(', ')' and '*' where '*' may represent '(', ')' or empty, determine whether the string can be a valid parentheses sequence. Track the possible range of open-bracket counts in one pass, or use two counter passes.

examples.explanation: The star can be treated as empty.
The star acts as an opening bracket.

title: N meetings in one room
description: Given start and end times of n meetings in one room, schedule the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings (a meeting must finish before the next begins; start time of the next must be strictly greater). Sort by end time and greedily pick compatible meetings.

examples.explanation: Hold the meetings ending at 2, 4, 7 and 9.

title: Jump Game - I
description: Given an array where each element is your maximum jump length from that position, determine whether you can reach the last index starting from the first. Keep one variable for the farthest reachable index and fail as soon as the current position passes it.

examples.explanation: Every path lands on the 0 at index 3.

title: Jump Game II
description: Given the same jump rules, return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index (it is always reachable). Greedily track the end of the current jump's range and the farthest the next jump can reach, counting a jump each time you cross the range boundary.

examples.explanation: Jump from index 0 to 1, then from 1 straight to the end.

title: Minimum number of platforms required for a railway
description: Given arrival and departure times of trains at a station, find the minimum number of platforms needed so no train waits. Sort arrivals and departures independently and sweep both lists like a merge, counting the running overlap maximum.

examples.explanation: Around 11:00 three trains occupy the station at once.

title: Job sequencing Problem
description: Given n jobs, each with a deadline (in time slots) and a profit earned when finished on or before the deadline, maximize total profit by scheduling at most one job per slot. Sort jobs by profit descending and place each into its latest free slot.

examples.explanation: Do the profit-40 job in slot 1 and the profit-20 job in slot 4.

title: Candy
description: Children in a row each get at least one candy; a child with a higher rating than an adjacent child must receive more candies. Find the minimum total candies with two passes: left-to-right for rising ratings, then right-to-left taking the max.

examples.explanation: The candy counts are [2, 1, 2].
The candy counts are [1, 2, 1].

title: Shortest Job First
description: Given CPU burst times of processes scheduled with Shortest Job First (non-preemptive), compute the average waiting time. Sorting the processes by burst time minimizes the cumulative wait; waiting time of each process is the sum of bursts before it.

examples.explanation: Order 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 gives waits 0, 1, 3, 6, 10 totalling 20 over 5 processes.

title: Program for Least Recently Used (LRU) Page Replacement Algorithm
description: Simulate the LRU page replacement policy: given a reference string of page requests and a fixed number of frames, count the page faults (a request for a page not currently in a frame). Track recency and evict the least recently used page on overflow.

examples.explanation: Hits on 0 (step 5), 0 (step 7), 3 and 2 at the end keep the fault count at 9.

title: Insert Interval
description: Given a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and one new interval, insert it so the result stays sorted and non-overlapping, merging any intervals it intersects. Collect intervals ending before the new one, merge all overlapping ones into it, then append the rest.

title: Merge Intervals
