description: Given a collection of intervals that may overlap, merge every overlapping pair and return the covering set of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start. Greedily sort by start and extend the current interval while the next one begins before it ends.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
description: Given an array of intervals, return the minimum number of intervals you must remove so that the remaining intervals do not overlap (touching at endpoints is allowed). Sort by end time and greedily keep every compatible interval, counting the skips.

examples.explanation: Removing [1, 3] leaves three intervals that only touch at endpoints.

title: Pre, Post, Inorder in one traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, produce its preorder, inorder and postorder traversals in a single pass. Use a stack of (node, state) pairs: state 1 emits preorder and pushes the node again with state 2, state 2 emits inorder and re-pushes with state 3, and state 3 emits postorder.

title: Preorder Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its preorder traversal (root, left subtree, right subtree). Implement both the recursive version and the iterative stack-based version where the root is popped, recorded, and its right child pushed before its left.

title: Inorder Traversal of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its inorder traversal (left subtree, root, right subtree). Implement both recursion and the iterative version: push left spine nodes onto a stack, pop, record, and move to the right child.

title: Postorder Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its postorder traversal (left subtree, right subtree, root). Implement both the recursive version and the iterative versions using two stacks or a single stack with a last-visited pointer.

title: Level Order Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its level order traversal: the values grouped level by level, left to right within each level. Process a queue one level at a time by snapshotting its current size, in O(n).

title: Iterative Preorder Traversal of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its preorder traversal without recursion. Use an explicit stack: pop a node, record it, push its right child and then its left child so the left subtree is processed first.

title: Iterative Inorder Traversal of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its inorder traversal without recursion. Use an explicit stack: descend pushing every left child, pop the deepest node, record it, and continue from its right child.

title: Post-order Traversal of Binary Tree using 2 stack
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its postorder traversal iteratively using two stacks. Push the root on stack 1; repeatedly pop from stack 1 into stack 2 while pushing the node's left then right children; stack 2 finally holds the postorder reversed.

title: Post-order Traversal of Binary Tree using 1 stack
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its postorder traversal iteratively using a single stack. Track the last visited node: while the current node exists push it and go left; otherwise peek the right child and traverse it only if it exists and was not just visited, else record the stack top.

title: Preorder, Inorder, and Postorder Traversal in one Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, compute its preorder, inorder and postorder traversals in one traversal pass. Use a stack of (node, visitNumber) tuples and emit the node into the corresponding list on visits 1, 2 and 3, descending left then right between visits.

title: Maximum Depth in BT
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth: the number of nodes along the longest root-to-leaf path. Compute it recursively as 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), or level-order with a counter, in O(n).

title: Check for balanced binary tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is height-balanced: for every node the depths of its two subtrees differ by at most 1. Return the height from each recursive call (or -1 as a failure flag) so the check completes in one O(n) pass.

examples.explanation: The left subtree is two levels deeper than the right at the root.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its diameter: the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes, which may not pass through the root. At each node the best path through it is leftHeight + rightHeight; track the maximum while returning heights.

examples.explanation: The path 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 (or 5 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3) uses 3 edges.

title: Maximum path sum
description: Given the root of a binary tree where node values may be negative, find the maximum path sum: the largest sum of values along any path between two nodes in the tree. Each recursion returns the best gain extending downward while updating the global answer with left + node + right.

examples.explanation: The path 15 -> 20 -> 7 sums to 42.

title: Check if two trees are identical or not
description: Given the roots of two binary trees, check whether they are identical: the same structure with the same values at every corresponding node. Recurse on both trees in lockstep (or compare their traversals), returning false at the first mismatch.

title: Zig Zag or Spiral Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its zigzag level order traversal: level 0 left to right, level 1 right to left, alternating each level. Process a normal level-order queue and reverse every second level (or use a deque inserting at alternating ends).

title: Boundary Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, print its boundary traversal: the root, then the left boundary (excluding leaves), then all leaves left to right, then the right boundary (excluding leaves) in reverse order. Handle single-node trees and children that make part of a boundary empty.

title: Vertical Order Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its vertical order traversal: nodes grouped by vertical column (root is 0, left child -1, right child +1), columns left to right, and within a column nodes ordered by level (row, then value as tiebreak). BFS carrying (column, row) labels each node.

title: Top View of BT
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its top view: the values visible looking down from above, i.e. the first node encountered at every horizontal distance column, ordered from leftmost column to rightmost. BFS with a column-keyed map gives the first per column.

title: Bottom view of BT
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its bottom view: the last node encountered at every horizontal distance column when viewed from below, ordered left to right. BFS (or DFS with depth tiebreaks) keeping the latest node per column works in O(n).

title: Right/Left View of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its right view: the last node of every level, i.e. the values visible from the right side. Take the final node of each level-order layer, or recurse right-first keeping the first node seen per depth.

examples.explanation: The left view analogously returns [1, 2, 5].

title: Symmetric Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is symmetric around its center: the left and right subtrees are mirror images. Compare mirrored node pairs recursively (or with a queue), checking value equality and cross-wise children.

title: Print root to leaf path in BT
description: Given the root of a binary tree, print every root-to-leaf path as a sequence of node values. Recurse carrying the current path, appending each node and printing when a leaf is reached; backtracking removes the node on the way up.

title: LCA in BT
description: Given the root of a binary tree and two nodes p and q, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both as descendants (a node may be an ancestor of itself). Recurse left and right; a node whose calls return both targets is the LCA, in O(n).

examples.explanation: Both 5 and 1 hang below the root 3.

title: Maximum Width of BT
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum width: the largest number of nodes present between the leftmost and rightmost non-null nodes on any level, counted with index arithmetic (children of index i are 2i and 2i+1). BFS with indices, using 64-bit arithmetic to avoid overflow.

examples.explanation: The last level spans indices 4 through 7, a width of 4.

title: Children Sum Property in Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, transform it so every node's value equals the sum of its children's values; you may only increase node values (never decrease), so a single root-to-leaf pass propagating children sums upward builds a valid tree in O(n).

examples.output: root becomes [150, 17, 110, 2, 15, 30, 80] style values where each parent equals its children's sum

title: Print all nodes at a distance of K in BT
description: Given the root of a binary tree, a target node and an integer k, return all node values at distance exactly k from the target, where edges connect a node to its parent and children. Build a parent map with one traversal, then BFS outward k levels from the target.

examples.explanation: 7 and 4 lie two edges below 5, and 1 is two edges above via the root.

title: Minimum time taken to burn the BT from a given Node
description: Given the root of a binary tree and a start node value, a fire starting there spreads to adjacent nodes every second; compute the minimum time to burn the entire tree. Map each node to its neighbours (including parents) and BFS level by level from the start.

examples.explanation: At t=1 nodes 1, 4, 5 catch fire and at t=2 the last node 3 does.

title: Count total nodes in a complete BT
description: Given the root of a complete binary tree, count its nodes in less than O(n) time. Compare the leftmost and rightmost spine heights: if equal the subtree has 2^h - 1 nodes, otherwise recurse on both halves, giving O(log^2 n).

title: Requirements needed to construct a unique BT
description: State the combinations of traversals that uniquely reconstruct a binary tree: inorder plus any one of preorder, postorder or level order is sufficient, while preorder with postorder alone leaves ambiguous trees. Explain why inorder's split property pins down the root's position.

title: Construct a BT from Preorder and Inorder
description: Given the preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree (values distinct), construct the tree. The first preorder element is the root; its inorder index splits left and right subtrees; recurse on the two halves using an index map for O(n).

title: Construct the Binary Tree from Postorder and Inorder Traversal
description: Given the postorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree (values distinct), construct the tree. The last postorder element is the root; its inorder index splits the subtrees; recurse right subtree first because postorder lists it before the left, using an index map for O(n).

title: Serialize and De-serialize BT
description: Design serialization: convert a binary tree to a string (for example preorder with null markers) and deserialize it back into the identical tree. Any format works as long as encode and decode are inverses; a queue consuming tokens rebuilds the tree in O(n).

examples.output: serialize(root) = '1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#', and deserialize returns the original tree

title: Morris Preorder Traversal of a Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, perform preorder traversal in O(n) time and O(1) extra space using Morris threading. Temporarily link each node's rightmost left-subtree descendant back to the node, follow the thread after the left subtree finishes, and remove the temporary link.

title: Morris Inorder Traversal of a Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, perform inorder traversal in O(n) time and O(1) extra space using Morris threading. Before descending left, find the predecessor (rightmost node of the left subtree) and thread it to the current node; when the thread is found again, record the current node and cut the thread.

title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
description: Given the root of a binary tree, flatten it into a 'linked list' in place: the list uses the right pointers only and follows preorder order, with every left pointer null. Reverse-think recursively (flatten right then left, relinking a global tail) or use Morris-style re-linking.

title: Search in a Binary Search Tree
description: Given the root of a binary search tree and a value, return the subtree rooted at the node with that value, or null if it is absent. Exploit BST ordering: go left when the value is smaller, right when larger, finishing in O(height).

title: Find Min/Max in BST
description: Given the root of a BST, find the node with the minimum value and the node with the maximum value. The minimum sits at the end of the leftmost path and the maximum at the end of the rightmost path; each is found in O(height).

title: Floor and Ceil in a BST
description: Given the root of a BST and a key, find its floor (largest value <= key) and ceil (smallest value >= key); return -1 for either if it does not exist. Walk down the tree remembering the best candidate each time the search moves away from it.

title: Floor in a Binary Search Tree
description: Given the root of a BST and a key, return the floor: the greatest value in the tree that is less than or equal to the key, or -1 when every value is larger. Descend the tree, updating the candidate floor whenever you branch right past a smaller value.

title: Insert a given node in BST
description: Given the root of a BST and a value, insert a new node with that value and return the root; duplicates are typically ignored. Attach the node at the null leaf where BST search terminates, in O(height).

examples.output: BST with 6 attached as the left child of 7

title: Delete a node in BST
description: Given the root of a BST and a key, delete the node with that key preserving the BST property. A leaf disappears directly; a one-child node is replaced by its child; a two-child node takes its inorder successor (or predecessor) in its place.

examples.explanation: The successor 4 replaces the deleted node 3.

title: Kth Smallest and Largest element in BST
description: Given the root of a BST and an integer k, return the k-th smallest and (optionally) the k-th largest value in the tree. The inorder traversal of a BST is sorted, so counting nodes during an inorder walk (or doing a reverse walk for largest) yields the answer in O(n).

examples.explanation: Inorder order is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and the third is 3.

title: Check if a tree is a BST or not
description: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid BST: every node's value lies strictly within the range allowed by its ancestors. Recurse with (min, max) bounds, or check that an inorder traversal is strictly increasing.

examples.explanation: 4 sits in the right subtree of 5 but is smaller than 5.

title: LCA in BST
description: Given the root of a BST and two nodes p and q, return their lowest common ancestor. Walk from the root: if both values are smaller go left, both larger go right, otherwise the current node splits them and is the LCA, in O(height).

title: Construct a BST from a preorder traversal
description: Given a preorder traversal of a BST (values distinct), reconstruct the unique tree. The first value is the root; elements smaller than it form the left subtree and the rest the right; a bound-based recursion or a stack of ancestors builds it in O(n).

examples.output: BST with root 8, left subtree 5 (children 1, 7), right subtree 10 (right child 12)

title: Inorder Successor/Predecessor in BST
description: Given the root of a BST and a key, find its inorder successor (smallest value greater than key) and predecessor (largest value smaller than key); return -1 when absent. Track candidates while descending: go right past smaller values for the predecessor, left past larger values for the successor.

title: Merge 2 BST's
description: Given the roots of two BSTs, merge them into one balanced BST containing all values. Collect the two sorted inorder sequences, merge them like merge sort into one sorted array, then build a balanced BST recursively from the middle element, in O(m + n).

examples.output: a balanced BST over the sorted values [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

title: Two Sum In BST | Check if there exists a pair with Sum K
description: Given the root of a BST and an integer k, determine whether two nodes exist whose values sum to k. Use two iterators (min stack and max stack) converging like a two-pointer scan over the sorted inorder in O(n), or a hashset during one traversal.

title: Correct BST with two nodes swapped
description: Given the root of a BST where exactly two nodes have been swapped by mistake, recover the tree without changing its structure. Do an inorder traversal, spot the two out-of-order values, and swap their node values back, in O(n) with O(h) space.

examples.explanation: 1 and 3 were swapped; restoring them repairs the BST.

title: Largest BST in Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the size of the largest subtree that is itself a BST. Post-order recursion returns (isBST, size, min, max) per subtree; a node forms a BST only when both children are BSTs and its value sits between their bounds.

examples.explanation: The subtree 5 -> (1, 8) is the largest BST.

title: Connected Components
description: Given the number of vertices and an edge list of an undirected graph, count the connected components: maximal groups of vertices reachable from one another. Iterate all vertices, launching BFS/DFS or a union-find merge from every unvisited vertex.

examples.explanation: {0, 1, 2} and {3, 4} are the two components.

title: Traversal Techniques
description: Implement the two core graph traversal techniques: BFS, which explores neighbours level by level using a queue, and DFS, which dives along one path using recursion or a stack. Given an adjacency list, produce the vertex order each technique visits from a source node.

title: DFS
description: Given an undirected graph as an adjacency list and a source vertex, print the depth-first search order: visit a vertex, recurse into its first unvisited neighbour, backtrack when stuck. Maintain a visited array so each vertex and edge is processed once, in O(V + E).

title: Number of provinces
description: Given an n x n adjacency matrix where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means direct friendship, return the number of provinces: connected components of friends (direct or transitive). Run DFS/BFS from every unvisited city or count union-find components, in O(n^2).

title: Connected Components Problem in Matrix
description: Given a binary matrix, count the groups of connected 1s (4-directional adjacency), the matrix analog of connected components. Scan every cell and flood-fill each unvisited 1 with BFS or DFS, incrementing the component count once per fill.

examples.explanation: The three 1s in the top-left corner form one component and the lone 1 another.

title: Rotten Oranges
description: Given a grid where 0 is empty, 1 is a fresh orange and 2 is a rotten orange, every rotten orange spoils adjacent fresh oranges each minute; return the minimum time until no fresh orange remains, or -1 if some can never rot. Multi-source BFS from all rotten oranges simultaneously.

examples.explanation: The orange at (2,0) is isolated by empty cells.

title: Flood fill algorithm
description: Given an image as a color grid, a starting pixel (sr, sc) and a new color, flood-fill: recolor the starting pixel and every 4-directionally connected pixel of the same original color. BFS or DFS from the start, stopping at color changes, in O(m*n).

title: Cycle Detection in Undirected Graph (bfs)
description: Given an undirected graph, detect whether it contains a cycle using BFS. Traverse from each unvisited vertex with a queue carrying (node, parent); encountering an already-visited neighbour that is not the current node's parent reveals a cycle, in O(V + E).

examples.explanation: The edges 0-1, 1-2 and 0-2 close a triangle.

title: Detect a cycle in an undirected graph
description: Given an undirected graph, detect whether it contains a cycle using DFS. Carry the parent through recursive calls; if any neighbour is already visited and is not the parent, a back edge closes a cycle, in O(V + E).

title: Distance of nearest cell having one
description: Given a binary matrix, replace every 0 with the distance to its nearest 1 (4-directional), leaving 1s as 0 distance. Push all 1s into a queue as multi-source BFS roots and expand outward, updating each newly reached 0 with its distance.

title: Surrounded Regions
description: Given a 2D board of X and O, flip every region of O that is fully surrounded by X into X; O regions touching the border are untouched. First mark border-connected O regions via DFS/BFS, then flip every remaining O, in O(m*n).

examples.explanation: The O at (3,1) touches the border and survives.

title: Number of enclaves
description: Given a binary grid where 1 is land, count the land cells from which you cannot walk off the grid boundary moving 4-directionally over land. Remove every land region touching the border (flood fill), then count the surviving 1s.

examples.explanation: The middle 1-region of three cells is enclosed.

title: Word ladder I
description: Given a beginWord, an endWord and a word list, transform beginWord into endWord one letter at a time with every intermediate word in the list; return the length of the shortest transformation sequence, or 0 if impossible. BFS over words with wildcard bucket neighbours.

examples.explanation: hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog uses five words.

title: Word ladder II
description: Return all shortest transformation sequences from beginWord to endWord (word ladder II). Build a BFS level graph recording each word's parents, then backtrack every path from endWord to beginWord through those parents.

examples.output: [hit, hot, dot, dog, cog] and [hit, hot, lot, log, cog]

title: Number of islands
description: Given a 2D grid of 1s (land) and 0s (water), count the islands: groups of 1s connected horizontally or vertically, surrounded by water. Scan the grid and sink each unvisited island with DFS/BFS, counting one island per fill, in O(m*n).

title: Bipartite Graph (DFS)
description: Given an undirected graph as an adjacency list, determine whether it is bipartite: the vertices can be split into two sets with every edge crossing between sets, i.e. the graph is 2-colorable. DFS-color vertices alternately; a conflicting neighbour means not bipartite.

examples.explanation: The triangle 0-1-2 cannot be 2-colored.

title: Cycle Detection in Directed Graph (DFS)
description: Given a directed graph, detect whether it contains a cycle using DFS with two state marks: visited and path-visited. Moving to a vertex already on the current recursion path finds a back edge and hence a cycle, in O(V + E).

examples.explanation: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1 is a directed cycle.

title: Topo Sort
description: Given a directed acyclic graph, produce a topological ordering: a linear order where every edge points forward. DFS from every unvisited vertex, pushing each vertex onto a stack as it finishes; the reversed stack is a valid topological order, in O(V + E).

title: Topological sort or Kahn's algorithm
description: Compute a topological ordering of a DAG using Kahn's BFS algorithm. Repeatedly take a vertex with in-degree 0 into the order and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees; the queue empties exactly when the graph is acyclic, in O(V + E).

title: Detect a cycle in a directed graph
description: Given a directed graph, detect a cycle using Kahn's algorithm: run the in-degree BFS and count how many vertices get processed. Fewer than V vertices processed means every remaining vertex is stuck in a cycle, in O(V + E).

title: Course Schedule I
description: Given numCourses and prerequisite pairs [course, prereq], determine whether all courses can be finished: the prerequisite relations form a directed graph and finishing is possible exactly when it has no cycle. Detect the cycle with DFS states or Kahn's algorithm.

title: Course Schedule II
description: Given numCourses and prerequisites, return any valid order to take all courses, or an empty array when impossible. The answer is a topological sort of the prerequisite graph, produced by Kahn's BFS or DFS with cycle detection.

title: Find eventual safe states
description: Given a directed graph where a terminal node has no outgoing edges, a safe node leads only to terminal nodes along every path; return all safe nodes in ascending order. Reverse the graph and run Kahn's algorithm on out-degrees: nodes whose outgoing edges all resolve are safe.

title: Alien Dictionary
description: Given a sorted list of words from an alien language, derive the character order of its alphabet; return '' when the order is impossible (a contradiction like a longer prefix first, or a cycle). Build precedence edges from adjacent word pairs and topologically sort them.

examples.explanation: t < f, w < e, r < t and e < r chain into the order w e r t f.

title: Shortest path in undirected graph with unit weights
description: Given an undirected unweighted graph and a source vertex, compute the shortest distance from the source to every other vertex, or -1 for unreachable ones. BFS explores level by level, so the first arrival at each vertex fixes its shortest distance, in O(V + E).

title: Shortest path in DAG
description: Given a weighted directed acyclic graph and a source, find the shortest distance to every vertex. Topologically sort the DAG, then relax edges in that order so each vertex is finalized before being used - no priority queue is needed, in O(V + E).

examples.explanation: Vertex 2 is cheaper via 0->4->2 (3) than via 0->1->2 (5).

title: Djisktra's Algorithm
description: Given a weighted graph (directed or undirected, non-negative weights) and a source, compute the shortest distance to every vertex using Dijkstra's algorithm. A min-heap repeatedly extracts the closest unfinalized vertex and relaxes its edges, in O(E log V).

examples.explanation: Reaching 2 through 1 costs 1 + 2 = 3, beating the direct edge 6.

title: Why priority Queue is used in Djisktra's Algorithm
description: Explain why Dijkstra's algorithm uses a priority queue: the greedy invariant requires always finalizing the currently closest unfinalized vertex, and a min-heap extracts it in O(log V). A plain queue loses the invariant and a sorted array scan costs O(V) per extraction; the heap keeps the total at O(E log V).

examples.output: the heap pops 0 (dist 0), then 1 (dist 1), then 2 (dist 3), finalizing each vertex at its true distance

title: Shortest Distance in a Binary Maze
description: Given a binary maze where 1 is an open cell and 0 is blocked, find the shortest path length from the source cell to the destination moving in 4 directions. Plain BFS works when every step costs 1; for a 0/1 maze variant use 0-1 BFS with a deque.

title: Path with minimum effort
description: Given a grid of heights, a route's effort is the maximum absolute difference in heights between two consecutive cells of the route; find the minimum possible effort walking from the top-left to the bottom-right cell. Binary search the effort with BFS/DFS checks, or run Dijkstra on the effort metric.

examples.explanation: The route 1 -> 2 -> 2 -> 2 -> 5 never jumps by more than 2.

title: Cheapest flight within K stops
description: Given n cities, priced flights (src, dst, price) and a limit of at most k stops (intermediate cities), find the cheapest price from src to dst or -1. Bellman-Ford limited to k+1 relaxation rounds, or a Dijkstra variant carrying remaining stops, solves it.

examples.explanation: 0 -> 1 -> 3 costs 100 + 600; the two-hop route through 2 violates the stop limit.

title: Network Delay Time
description: Given directed signal travel times times[i] = (u, v, w) from node u to v, return the time when all n nodes receive a signal sent from node k, or -1 if some node is unreachable. This is single-source Dijkstra over a directed graph; the answer is the maximum distance.

examples.explanation: Node 1 is reached last, via 2 -> 3 -> 1, taking 2 time units.

title: Number of ways to arrive at destination
description: Given a weighted undirected graph with the shortest distance between the source (node 0) and destination (node n-1) fixed, count the number of distinct shortest paths, modulo 10^9 + 7. Run Dijkstra storing both distance and ways: an equal-distance arrival adds the predecessor's count.

examples.explanation: 0 -> 1 -> 4 and 0 -> 3 -> 4 are the two shortest routes.

title: Minimum multiplications to reach end
description: Given a start number, an end number and an array of multipliers, each move replaces the current number with (current * multiplier) mod 100000; find the minimum number of multiplications needed to reach the end. BFS over the value graph treats numbers as nodes and multiplications as edges.

title: Bellman Ford Algorithm
description: Given a directed weighted graph that may contain negative edges (no negative cycles) and a source, compute shortest distances using Bellman-Ford: relax every edge V-1 times. If a V-th relaxation still improves a distance, report a negative cycle, in O(V*E).

title: Floyd warshall algorithm
description: Given the edge-weight matrix of a directed graph, compute all-pairs shortest paths with the Floyd-Warshall DP: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]) for every intermediate k. Negative edges are fine; negative cycles show as negative diagonal entries, in O(V^3).

examples.input: matrix = [[0, 5, INF, 10], [INF, 0, 3, INF], [INF, INF, 0, 1], [INF, INF, INF, 0]]

title: Find the city with the smallest number of neighbors
description: Given n cities and weighted edges, a city's reach is the number of other cities within the distanceThreshold; return the city with the smallest reach, preferring the larger city number on ties. Compute all-pairs distances with Floyd-Warshall and count reachable neighbours per city.

examples.explanation: City 3 reaches only city 2 within the threshold.

title: Prim's Algorithm
description: Given a connected weighted undirected graph, build its minimum spanning tree with Prim's algorithm: grow the tree from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge that connects a tree vertex to an outside vertex, using a priority queue, in O(E log V).

title: Disjoint Set
description: Implement a Disjoint Set Union (union-find) structure with find (with path compression) and union (by rank or size). Both operations run in nearly O(1) amortized, powering cycle detection and component queries in Kruskal's MST and dynamic connectivity problems.

examples.output: find(1) == find(3), while find(4) sits in a different set

title: Find the MST weight
description: Given a weighted undirected graph, return the total weight of its minimum spanning tree. Sort the edges by weight and add each edge that connects two different components (checked with union-find) until the tree spans all vertices - Kruskal's algorithm, in O(E log E).

examples.explanation: The MST picks edges 0-2 (1) and 1-2 (3).

title: Number of operations to make network connected
description: Given n computers and direct cable connections, return the minimum number of cables to move so every computer connects into one network, or -1 if there are too few cables. Count components with union-find; (components - 1) moves are needed when spare cables suffice.

examples.explanation: One redundant cable can be moved to connect computer 3.

title: Most stones removed with same row or column
description: Stones sit on a 2D plane; a move removes a stone that shares its row or column with another stone. Return the maximum number of stones removable. Stones in the same row/column form connected components, and each component of size s yields s - 1 removals, solved with union-find.

examples.explanation: Every stone except one anchor can be removed.

title: Accounts merge
description: Given accounts where each account is a name plus its emails, merge accounts that share any email (same person), returning merged accounts with emails sorted. Union-find (or DFS over an email graph) groups emails by person, in O(total emails * alpha).

title: Number of islands II
description: Given an m x n water grid and a sequence of land-adding positions, report the number of islands after each addition (online island counting). Union-find merges each new land cell with its 4-directional neighbours, adjusting the component count as unions occur.

title: Making a large island
description: Given a binary grid of 0s and 1s, you may change at most one 0 to 1; return the size of the largest island possible. Label each island with union-find or DFS, then for every 0 sum the distinct neighbouring island sizes plus one, in O(n^2).

examples.explanation: Flipping either 0 connects the two islands into one of size 3.

title: Swim in Rising Water
description: Given an n x n elevation grid where you can move to a neighbouring cell only when its elevation is at most the current water level, find the minimum time (water level) at which you can travel from the top-left to the bottom-right cell. Binary search the level with BFS checks, or use a min-heap Dijkstra-style traversal.

examples.explanation: You must wait until the level reaches 3 to enter the bottom-right cell.

title: Bridges in graph
description: Given an undirected graph, find all its bridges: edges whose removal disconnects the graph. Use Tarjan's algorithm - DFS with discovery times and low-link values; an edge (u, v) is a bridge when low[v] > disc[u], in O(V + E).

examples.explanation: Removing either edge separates vertices 3/4 from the rest.

title: Articulation point in graph
description: Given an undirected graph, find all articulation points: vertices whose removal (with their edges) disconnects the graph. DFS with discovery times and low-link values flags a vertex when a child subtree cannot reach above it (root case: two or more DFS children), in O(V + E).

examples.explanation: Removing 0 isolates the 3-4 pair; removing 3 isolates 4.

title: Kosaraju's algorithm
description: Given a directed graph, count its strongly connected components (SCCs) with Kosaraju's algorithm: order vertices by finishing time in a DFS, then DFS the reversed graph in that order; each DFS tree in the second pass is one SCC, in O(V + E).

examples.explanation: The SCCs are {0, 1, 2}, {3} and {4}.

title: Climbing stairs
description: You are climbing a staircase with n steps and can climb either 1 or 2 steps at a time; count the number of distinct ways to reach the top. The recurrence ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2) makes this a Fibonacci-style DP in O(n) with O(1) space.

examples.explanation: The ways are 1+1+1, 1+2 and 2+1.

title: Frog Jump
description: A frog starts on stone 0 of a row of stones and may jump to the next stone or skip one stone; each jump costs the absolute difference of the stone heights. Find the minimum total energy to reach the last stone. DP over positions with the two-jump recurrence, in O(n) time.

title: Frog jump with K distances
description: The frog may now jump anywhere from 1 to k stones ahead, paying the absolute height difference for each jump; find the minimum energy to reach the last stone. The DP checks the last k predecessors of each position, giving O(n*k).

title: Maximum sum of non adjacent elements
description: Given an array of positive integers, find the maximum sum of elements such that no two chosen elements are adjacent in the array. The DP keeps the best sum ending at each index including or excluding it, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

examples.explanation: Pick 2 and 9 for a total of 11.

title: House robber
description: Houses in a circle each hold money, but robbing two adjacent houses triggers an alarm; maximize the loot where the first and last houses are also adjacent. Solve two linear subproblems - houses 0..n-2 and 1..n-1 - with the non-adjacent DP and take the better result.

examples.explanation: Robbing house 1 alone is best because 0 and 2 are adjacent in the circle.

title: Ninja's training
description: A ninja trains for n days choosing one of three tasks each day, gaining the task's merit points, but never the same task on two consecutive days. Maximize total merit with DP carrying (day, lastTask), in O(n*3*3).

examples.explanation: Take task 2 on day 0 (5), task 0 on day 1 (3) and any task worth 3 on day 2.

title: Grid Unique Paths : DP on Grids (DP8)
description: A robot starts at the top-left of an m x n grid and moves only right or down; count the number of unique paths to the bottom-right cell. Paths(i, j) = paths(i-1, j) + paths(i, j-1), computed by DP in O(m*n) or combinatorially as C(m+n-2, m-1).

title: Unique paths II
description: Count unique top-left to bottom-right paths in a grid where cells marked 1 are obstacles the robot cannot enter; movement is still only right or down. The same DP passes the value 0 through obstacle cells, with mod arithmetic if required.

examples.explanation: Every path must skirt the central obstacle, leaving exactly two routes.

title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
description: Given an n x n matrix of integers, start anywhere in the top row and move to the row below choosing the same column or an adjacent one; find the minimum path sum to the bottom row. DP left-to-right with min over the up-to-three predecessors, in O(n^2).

examples.explanation: The path 1 -> 5 -> 7 sums to 13.

title: Triangle
description: Given a triangle of numbers, find the minimum path sum from the apex to the base, moving from each cell to one of the two cells directly below it. Bottom-up DP over rows - triangle[i][j] += min(triangle[i+1][j], triangle[i+1][j+1]) - runs in O(n^2) and O(1) extra space.

examples.explanation: The path 2 -> 3 -> 5 -> 1 sums to 11.

title: Ninja and his Friends
description: Two friends start at the top-left and top-right corners of an m x n grid and move down one row each step, each drifting at most one column sideways; both collect their cell's points, sharing a cell's points only once. Maximize the combined points with 3D DP over (row, colA, colB), in O(m*n^2).

examples.explanation: The two walkers together sweep up the central 5s on the way down.

title: Subset sum equal to target (DP- 14)
description: Given an array of non-negative integers and a target sum, determine whether some subset of the elements adds up exactly to the target. Subset-sum DP over (index, remaining target) with take/skip choices, in O(n*target) time.

examples.explanation: The element 4 itself, or 1 + 3, hits the target.

title: Partition equal subset sum
description: Given a positive integer array, decide whether it can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sums. The total must be even, and the question reduces to subset-sum with target = total/2, solvable with a bitset or boolean DP in O(n*total/2).

examples.explanation: The subsets [1, 5, 5] and [11] both sum to 11.

title: Partition a set into two subsets with minimum absolute sum difference
description: Given a positive integer array, split it into two subsets S1 and S2 minimizing |S1 - S2| in sums. Run subset-sum DP up to total/2 recording which sums are reachable; the best reachable sum closest to total/2 gives the minimum difference.

examples.explanation: [1, 4] and [2, 3] both sum to 5.
The best split is {8} versus {6, 5} with sums 8 and 11.

title: Count subsets with sum K
description: Given an array of non-negative integers and a target k, count the subsets whose elements sum exactly to k. DP over (index, remaining sum) adds the take and skip branches instead of OR-ing them, all modulo 10^9 + 7 if required.

examples.explanation: The subsets are [1, 2], [1, 2] (the other 2) and [3].

title: Count partitions with given difference
description: Given an array and a difference d, count the partitions into two subsets S1 (larger) and S2 with S1 - S2 = d. Since S1 = (total + d) / 2 is fixed, the problem becomes counting subsets with that sum via DP (return 0 when the expression is not a valid integer).

examples.explanation: Subsets summing to 6 are [2, 4] and [1, 2, 3], each pairing with a complement subset.

title: Assign Cookies
description: Children each have a greed factor and cookies each have a size; a child is content when a cookie is at least their greed, and each child gets at most one cookie. Maximize content children by sorting both arrays and greedily matching the smallest sufficient cookie to each child, in O(n log n + m log m).

title: Minimum Coins (DP - 20)
description: Given coin denominations (infinite supply of each) and a target amount, find the minimum number of coins that make up the amount, or -1 when impossible. Unbounded-knapsack DP over amounts - dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin]) - runs in O(n*amount).

examples.explanation: 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 uses three coins.

title: Target sum
description: Given an array of numbers, assign '+' or '-' before each so the expression sums to target S; count the number of ways. The transformation S1 - S2 = S with S1 + S2 = total fixes S1, reducing the count to a subset-sum count DP over (total + S) / 2.

examples.explanation: Exactly one of the five 1s must be negative, giving five ways.

title: Coin Change 2 (DP - 22)
description: Given coin denominations (infinite supply) and an amount, count the distinct combinations (order does not matter) that form the amount. Iterate coins in the outer loop of the 1D DP so each combination is counted once, in O(n*amount).

examples.explanation: The combinations are 5, 2+2+1, 2+1+1+1 and 1+1+1+1+1.

title: Unbounded knapsack
description: Given item weights and values with unlimited copies of each item, fill a knapsack of capacity W maximizing total value. Unbounded-knapsack DP iterates amounts upward so an item can be reused: dp[w] = max(dp[w], val + dp[w - wt]).

examples.explanation: Packing one 2-weight and two 4-weight items yields 5 + 11 + 11 = 27.

title: Rod Cutting Problem | (DP - 24)
description: Given the price of a rod piece of every integer length up to n, cut the rod into pieces (possibly none) to maximize total revenue. Unbounded-knapsack DP: dp[len] = max(price[i] + dp[len - i]) over all piece lengths i, in O(n^2).

examples.explanation: Cutting lengths 2 and 6 earns 5 + 17 = 22.

title: Longest common subsequence
description: Given two strings, find the length of their longest common subsequence (LCS): the longest sequence appearing in both with relative order preserved, not necessarily contiguously. DP over (i, j) - match extends the diagonal, otherwise take the best of skipping either character - in O(m*n).

examples.explanation: 'adb' is common to both strings.

title: Print Longest Common Subsequence | (DP - 26)
description: Given two strings, print one of their longest common subsequences. Build the standard LCS DP table, then walk from (0, 0): matching characters emit and move diagonally, otherwise step toward the larger neighbour, reconstructing the string in O(m + n).

title: Longest common substring
description: Given two strings, find the length of the longest common substring: the longest run of identical consecutive characters appearing in both. DP over (i, j) resets to zero on mismatch and extends the diagonal run on match, tracking the global maximum, in O(m*n).

examples.explanation: 'cjk' is the longest common substring.

title: Longest palindromic subsequence
description: Given a string, find the length of the longest palindromic subsequence (not necessarily contiguous). It equals the LCS of the string with its reverse, or can be computed directly with interval DP over (i, j), in O(n^2).

examples.explanation: 'babcbab' is the longest palindromic subsequence.

title: Minimum insertions to make string palindrome | DP-29
description: Given a string, find the minimum number of characters to insert anywhere so the result is a palindrome. The answer is n minus the longest palindromic subsequence length, since characters around an LPS skeleton need mirrors, in O(n^2).

examples.explanation: Keeping the LPS 'aca' (or 'aba'), two insertions mirror the leftovers.

title: Minimum insertions or deletions to convert string A to B
description: Given strings s1 and s2, find the minimum number of insertions and deletions on s1 required to transform it into s2. With L = LCS length, the answer is (m - L) deletions plus (n - L) insertions, computed in O(m*n).

examples.explanation: Delete b and d, keep a and c, then insert n.

title: Shortest common supersequence
description: Given two strings, build the shortest string that has both as subsequences (the shortest common supersequence). Its length is m + n - LCS; walk the LCS DP table emitting characters from both strings while following the common skeleton, in O(m*n).

title: Distinct subsequences
description: Given strings s and t, count the distinct subsequences of s that equal t. DP over (i, j): dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + (match ? dp[i-1][j-1] : 0), counting how many ways the suffix of s covers the suffix of t, in O(m*n).

examples.explanation: 'bag' hides in 'babgbag' five different ways.

title: Edit distance
description: Given two words, return the minimum number of operations (insert, delete or replace a character) to convert word1 into word2. Classic edit distance DP over (i, j): a match costs nothing, otherwise pay one plus the best of insert, delete or replace, in O(m*n).

examples.explanation: horse -> rorse (replace h) -> rose (remove r) -> ros (remove e).

title: Wildcard matching
description: Given a string s and pattern p where '?' matches any single character and '*' matches any sequence (including empty), decide whether the pattern matches the entire string. DP over (i, j) with a special branch for '*' consuming zero or more characters, in O(m*n).

examples.explanation: The leading '*' absorbs 'ad' and the inner '*' absorbs 'ce'.

title: Best time to buy and sell stock
description: Given daily stock prices, complete at most one buy followed by one sell and return the maximum profit (0 when prices only fall). Track the minimum price so far and the best difference achievable today, in one O(n) pass.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1, sell at 6.

title: Best time to buy and sell stock II
description: Given daily stock prices, you may complete as many transactions as you like (buy before you sell, one holding at a time); maximize total profit. Every upward consecutive price difference can be captured, or run a two-state (hold / free) DP, in O(n).

examples.explanation: Buy at 1 sell at 5 (+4), then buy at 3 sell at 6 (+3).

title: Best time to buy and sell stock III
description: Given daily stock prices, complete at most two transactions (non-overlapping buy-sell pairs) and maximize total profit. DP tracks the best profit after first buy, first sell, second buy and second sell in one sweep, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

examples.explanation: Buy at 0 sell at 3 (+3), then buy at 1 sell at 4 (+3).

title: Best time to buy and sell stock IV
description: Given daily stock prices and a limit k on transactions, maximize profit with at most k buy-sell pairs. DP over (day, transactions used, holding) states - or buy/sell profit arrays per transaction tier - in O(n*k).

examples.explanation: Buy at 2 sell at 6 (+4), then buy at 0 sell at 3 (+3).

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
description: Given daily stock prices, maximize profit with unlimited transactions but a mandatory one-day cooldown after each sell (no buy on the day right after selling). DP over three states - holding, just sold, free - transitioning in O(n).

examples.explanation: Buy at 1 sell at 2, cooldown, buy at 0 sell at 2.

title: Best time to buy and sell stock with transaction fees
description: Given daily stock prices and a fixed transaction fee per completed sale, maximize profit with unlimited transactions. DP with hold/free states where each sell subtracts the fee, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1 sell at 8 (net +5), buy at 4 sell at 9 (net +3).

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description: Given an integer array, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (elements keep order but need not be adjacent). The O(n^2) DP keeps the best LIS ending at each index; patience sorting with binary search improves it to O(n log n).

examples.explanation: The subsequence 2, 3, 7, 101 is longest.

title: Print Longest Increasing Subsequence
description: Given an integer array, print one longest strictly increasing subsequence. Store a predecessor index alongside each DP value while computing LIS lengths, then backtrack from the best index to recover the actual elements, in O(n^2).

examples.explanation: This chain of length 3 is a longest increasing subsequence.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence |(DP-43)
description: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence in O(n log n) using the patience-sorting/tails-array method: binary-search each element's position in the tails array, replacing an existing tail or appending a new one.

examples.explanation: The tails array grows to [2, 3, 7, 101] and never needs a fifth slot.

title: Largest Divisible Subset
description: Given a set of distinct positive integers, return the largest subset in which every pair (a, b) has a % b == 0 or b % a == 0. Sort the array, DP the longest divisible chain ending at each index with predecessor links, then backtrack to print the subset, in O(n^2).

title: Longest String Chain
description: A word a is a predecessor of word b when inserting exactly one letter into a produces b; a chain uses each word at most once. Given a list of words, find the length of the longest possible chain. Sort by length and DP with a hashmap from word to best chain length, in O(n*L^2).

examples.explanation: The chain a -> ba -> bda -> bdca inserts one letter each time.

title: Longest Bitonic Subsequence
description: A bitonic subsequence first strictly increases then strictly decreases (either part may be empty). Given an array, find the length of its longest bitonic subsequence: for each index add the best increasing-run ending there to the best decreasing-run starting there, minus one, in O(n^2).

examples.explanation: The sequence 1, 2, 10, 4, 2, 1 rises then falls.

title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequences
description: Given an integer array, count the number of longest strictly increasing subsequences. DP stores (length, count) per index; when a chain of equal length is found, counts add up, and the final answer sums counts of maximal length, in O(n^2).

examples.explanation: Both 1, 3, 5, 7 and 1, 3, 4, 7 have length 4.

title: Matrix chain multiplication
description: Given the dimensions of n matrices (an array where arr[i-1] x arr[i] is matrix i), find the minimum number of scalar multiplications to multiply the whole chain. Partition DP: split the range at every k, multiply the two halves, and pay arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j] for the merge, in O(n^3) with memoization.

title: Matrix Chain Multiplication | Bottom-Up|(DP-49)
description: Solve matrix chain multiplication bottom-up with tabulation instead of memoization. Fill the DP table for shorter ranges first so every split cost dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j] is already available, in O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space.

title: Minimum cost to cut the stick
description: A stick of length n must be cut at the given cut positions (in order chosen by you); each cut costs the current length of the piece being cut. Find the minimum total cost by partition DP over the sorted cut points (with 0 and n as sentinels), in O(m^3).

examples.explanation: Cutting 4, 3, 5, 1 (in that chosen order) costs 7 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 16.

title: Burst balloons
description: Given balloons with numbers, bursting balloon i earns nums[left] * nums[i] * nums[right] using its current neighbours (1 outside the array); find the maximum coins from bursting all balloons. Interval DP decides the LAST balloon burst in each range, avoiding neighbour invalidation, in O(n^3).

examples.explanation: Bursting 1, 5, 3, 8 in that order maximizes the coins.

title: Different Ways to Evaluate a Boolean Expression
description: Given an expression string of digits and the operators +, -, *, return all possible results from evaluating it under every possible parenthesization. Recursively split at each operator, compute the result sets of both sides, and combine every pair, in exponential time bounded by Catalan numbers.

title: Palindrome partitioning II
description: Given a string, split it into the fewest palindromic substrings and return that minimum number of cuts. Precompute a palindrome table with expand-around-center or interval DP, then run a min-cut DP over cut positions, in O(n^2).

examples.explanation: One cut separates 'aa' from 'b'.

title: Partition Array for Maximum Sum
description: Given an integer array and a length limit k, partition it into contiguous groups of length at most k; each group's value becomes its maximum element times the group length. Maximize the total array sum after this transformation with partition DP, in O(n*k).

title: Maximum Rectangle Area with all 1's|(DP-55)
description: Given a binary matrix of 0s and 1s, find the area of the largest rectangle containing only 1s. Process each row as a histogram base (heights reset at 0s) and run the largest-rectangle-in-histogram stack algorithm per row, in O(n*m).

examples.explanation: A 2 x 3 all-ones rectangle spans rows 1-2, columns 2-4.

title: Count Square Submatrices with All Ones|(DP-56)
description: Given a matrix of 0s and 1s, count the square submatrices (of every size) whose entries are all 1s. DP over cells: dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) when the cell is 1, and the answer is the sum of all dp values, in O(n*m).

examples.explanation: There are ten 1x1, four 2x2 and one 3x3 all-ones squares.

title: Trie Implementation and Operations
description: Implement a trie (prefix tree) with insert(word), search(word) and startsWith(prefix), each in O(L) time. Each node holds a child map (or 26-slot array) and an end-of-word flag; walk the tree character by character for every operation.

examples.explanation: 'apple' is stored exactly, while 'app' exists only as a prefix.

title: Trie Implementation and Advanced Operations
description: Extend the trie with advanced operations: countWordsEqualTo(word), countWordsStartingWith(prefix) and erase(word). Store word-count and prefix-count fields on every node, incrementing along insert paths and decrementing along erase paths, all in O(L).

examples.input: insert('samsung'), insert('samsung'), insert('samsung'), countWordsEqualTo('samsung'), erase('samsung'), countWordsStartingWith('sams')
examples.explanation: Counts are tracked per node, so erasing one copy drops both totals.

title: Longest Word with All Prefixes
description: Given a list of words, return the longest word that can be built one character at a time such that every prefix of the word is also in the list; prefer the lexicographically smallest on ties. Insert everything into a trie and DFS only through nodes marked end-of-word, in O(total characters).

examples.explanation: 'apple' has all prefixes 'a', 'ap', 'app', 'appl' present, beating 'apply' lexicographically.

title: Number of distinct substrings in a string
description: Given a string, count its distinct substrings (excluding the empty string unless the variant includes it). Insert every suffix into a trie; each new node created corresponds to exactly one distinct substring, giving O(n^2) time and space (or use a suffix automaton for O(n)).

examples.output: 6 non-empty substrings (a, b, c, ab, bc, abc); 7 if the empty string is counted

title: Bit PreRequisites for TRIE Problems
description: Learn the bit-level vocabulary needed for trie problems: store integers as fixed-width binary strings (MSB first, usually 31 or 32 bits), insert/query by walking bits, and note how a binary trie finds maximum-XOR partners by preferring the opposite bit at the highest differing position.

examples.output: walking their paths diverges at bit 3, so XORing them yields a high-order 1 - the trie exploits exactly this

title: Maximum XOR of two numbers in an array
description: Given an array of non-negative integers, return the maximum result of nums[i] XOR nums[j] where i != j. Insert each number into a binary trie (MSB first); for each number greedily walk toward the opposite bit at every level to build the largest possible XOR partner, in O(n * 31).

examples.explanation: 5 XOR 25 = 28 is the largest pair XOR.

title: Maximum Xor with an element from an array
description: Given an array of non-negative integers and queries [xi, mi], for each query return the maximum XOR of xi with any array element at most mi, or -1 when every element exceeds mi. Sort both numbers and queries by value, insert elements into a binary trie as they become eligible, and answer greedily, in O((n + q) log max).

examples.explanation: For x=5, m=6 the element 2 gives 5 XOR 2 = 7.

title: Minimum number of bracket reversals to make an expression balanced
description: Given a string of '(' and ')' characters, find the minimum number of brackets you must reverse (flip between '(' and ')') to make the string balanced, or -1 if impossible (odd length). After cancelling matched pairs, ceil(remaining opens / 2) + ceil(remaining closes / 2) reversals suffice.

examples.explanation: Reverse both characters to get '()', which is balanced.

title: Count and say
description: The count-and-say sequence reads the previous term aloud: '1' becomes 'one 1' = '11', which becomes 'two 1s' = '21', and so on. Given n, produce the n-th term of the sequence starting from '1' as term 1.

examples.explanation: Term 3 is '21', read as 'one 2, one 1' giving '1211'.

title: Rabin Karp Algorithm
description: Implement the Rabin-Karp string matching algorithm: find all occurrence indices of a pattern in a text using a rolling polynomial hash so each window hash is updated in O(1). Verify candidate matches character-by-character to rule out hash collisions.

examples.explanation: The pattern's hash matches only the window starting at index 3, which verifies exactly.

title: Z function
description: Given a string s, compute its Z-array where z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting at i that is also a prefix of s. Maintain the rightmost matching window [l, r] and copy previously computed values inside it, computing fresh values only outside, in O(n).

examples.explanation: z[4] = 3 because the substring starting at index 4 is 'aba', matching the prefix.

title: KMP Algorithm or LPS array
description: Implement the KMP string matching algorithm: build the LPS (longest proper prefix which is also suffix) array of the pattern, then scan the text skipping re-comparisons using the failure links. Matching runs in O(n + m) time.

examples.explanation: The LPS array lets the scan jump back without re-examining text characters.

title: Shortest Palindrome
description: Given a string s, you may prepend characters to it; return the shortest palindrome obtainable this way. Reverse the string, append it after a separator, and use the LPS/KMP failure function of the combined string to find the longest palindromic prefix of s.

examples.explanation: Prepending 'dcb' makes the whole string a palindrome.

title: Longest happy prefix
description: A happy prefix is a proper prefix that is also a suffix of the string. Given a string, return the longest happy prefix, or the empty string if none exists. Solve it with the KMP LPS array in O(n).

examples.explanation: 'abab' is both a proper prefix and a suffix.

title: Count Palindromic Subsequences
description: Given a string of lowercase letters, count all palindromic subsequences (subsequences need not be contiguous). Use interval DP: dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j] + dp[i][j-1] - dp[i+1][j-1], adding the inner count once more when the end letters match, all modulo a large prime as required.

examples.explanation: The palindromic subsequences are 'a' (twice), 'b' and 'aa'.
